articles.title: ‘Papa, please save me’: Shekhar Suman remembers son Aayush’s final moments at 11, recalls the heartbreaking plea that still haunts him, and opens up about grief and financial struggles
articles.summary: Actor and television presenter Shekhar Suman has revisited one of the most painful chapters of his life, recalling how he continued working while his
articles.body: Actor and television presenter Shekhar Suman has revisited one of the most painful chapters of his life, recalling how he continued working while his eldest son, Aayush, battled a terminal illness. In a conversation with The Lallantop, Shekhar spoke about the family’s struggle during the child’s final days, the financial difficulties he faced at the time and the words Aayush spoke shortly before his death at the age of 11. The actor said the loss continues to affect his family, even decades later.For Shekhar, the period was marked by two devastating realities. He had little work and was worried about supporting his family when he learnt that his son was terminally ill. At a time when he felt he had little left to hold on to, he had to keep working while coping with the possibility of losing his child.‘I was completely ruined’: A father facing two crisesRecalling the moment he learnt about Aayush’s condition, Shekhar described how the news came when his professional life was already uncertain. “I discovered my son was terminally ill. Firstly, I had no work at that time. On top of that, we received such tragic news. I was completely ruined and destroyed. I thought I had nothing left in life,” he said during the interview. He also spoke about the financial pressure he was under, explaining that he was not earning enough to comfortably meet his son’s medical needs and did not want to depend on his family for money.Despite the circumstances, Shekhar was initially reluctant to work in television. He hoped for film offers, but calls from the industry often brought proposals for serials instead. That changed when director Anand Mahendroo approached him for the comedy show Dekh Bhai Dekh. Shekhar said he was hesitant at first, but Mahendroo encouraged him to reconsider, pointing out that Jaya Bachchan was producing the show. Shekhar eventually accepted the role, which became a significant part of his television career.Working on a comedy show while fearing the worstEven as his career found a new direction, the situation at home remained difficult. Shekhar said Aayush’s health was deteriorating, leaving him anxious throughout the working day. The production team kept a telephone on the set so that his family could contact him with updates. Every time it rang, he would answer with a pounding heart, afraid that he might hear bad news. After the call, however, he had to return to performing in a light-hearted comedy show.“I still don’t know how I did it all (continued working),” he recalled, describing the emotional difficulty of switching between his personal crisis and his professional responsibilities. For Shekhar, continuing to work was not simply about building a career. He felt responsible for supporting his family, even as he struggled to process what was happening to his son.‘Papa, I don’t want to go’: Aayush’s final wordsAmong the memories that have stayed with Shekhar is the moment he says occurred shortly before Aayush died. The actor recalled that his 11-year-old son had begun reciting Sanskrit shlokas. Shekhar said Aayush spoke about seeing a golden light, held his father’s hand and pleaded with him. “He said he saw a golden light coming, held my hand and told me, ‘Papa, I don’t want to go. Please save me.’ Then he started reciting some Sanskrit shlokas, and we were flustered,” Shekhar said.He added that Aayush then told the people gathered around him, including the family’s driver, that he loved them. “He was like an angel; he was a beautiful child,” the actor said. Shekhar described the loss as a tragedy that has never stopped hurting. He said he and his family still spend two to three hours each day thinking and talking about Aayush. “I still don’t know how that tragedy happened to us. But I guess that’s destiny. There’s no bigger tragedy that can befall parents than losing their children,” he said, adding that the wound would never fully heal.‘We will fight till the end’: The family’s most painful decisionShekhar also recalled how Aayush’s condition became so severe that his wife, Alka Suman, asked doctors to let their son go, believing he was suffering unbearably. The actor said he initially resisted the idea, telling her that they would continue fighting for their child. But he later acknowledged how difficult it had been for the family to watch Aayush endure so much pain. “She was the ‘savvy mother who begged for her son’s death.’ She was right; we couldn’t bear seeing him suffer like that,” he said.After Aayush’s death, Shekhar said he lost interest in work, money and fame. He continued working because he had to care for the rest of his family. His recollections offer a glimpse into a grief that has remained part of his life. For the actor, professional success could not erase the loss, and the memories of his son continue to occupy a deeply personal place in the family’s everyday life.You use AI every day. articles.title: Arnold Schwarzenegger’s childhood home became a museum after an investor bought it for about $656,000; it now welcomes visitors to explore his bodybuilding, film and political career
articles.summary: Arnold Schwarzenegger grew up in a modest house in Thal, near Graz in Austria.
articles.body: Arnold Schwarzenegger grew up in a modest house in Thal, near Graz in Austria. Decades later, the building became a museum dedicated to his journey from a young bodybuilding enthusiast to a Hollywood action star and California governor. Austrian investor Christian Baha acquired the former family residence at auction in 2009 for a reported €460,000, equivalent to about US$656,000 at the time. Some contemporary reports put the purchase price closer to €500,000. The building opened as a museum in 2011 and now displays personal belongings and memorabilia from different stages of Schwarzenegger’s life. Visitors can explore his childhood living conditions and discover objects linked to his bodybuilding achievements, Hollywood career and time as California governor. The museum offers fans a glimpse into the humble beginnings of one of Hollywood’s most recognisable stars.Arnold Schwarzenegger’s family once lived in this former police residenceThe building stands at Linakstrasse 9 in Thal, in Austria’s Styria region. Built in 1806, it originally served as a forester’s house associated with the Counts of Herberstein. It later became the official residence of the local gendarmerie commander. Schwarzenegger’s father, Gustav Schwarzenegger, worked as a police officer and lived there with his family. They occupied the upper floor while another family lived downstairs. The house was not owned by the Schwarzeneggers. It was official accommodation linked to his father’s position. The residence offered a glimpse of a very different life from the one Arnold would eventually lead. The museum preserves elements of that setting to help visitors understand his early years.What life was like for Arnold Schwarzenegger in ThalSchwarzenegger was born on July 30, 1947, in Graz and spent his childhood and teenage years in Thal. His mother, Aurelia, managed the household while his father served in the local police. According to the museum’s historical account, the family initially lived without running water and electricity. They had to carry water and firewood into the house each day. The kitchen and other parts of the residence reflected the modest conditions of the period. Schwarzenegger’s interest in sport developed during his youth. He began bodybuilding as a teenager and soon set his sights on international competition. On August 8, 1966, at the age of 19, he left the family home to pursue opportunities in Munich. That decision marked the beginning of a career that would take him far beyond his Austrian hometown.How an investor helped turn the house into a museumThe property was privately owned before it was acquired in 2009. Austrian investor Christian Baha, the founder of Superfund, helped secure the building for its new purpose. Contemporary Austrian reporting put the purchase price at approximately €460,000, while a later report from Austrian broadcaster ORF cited a figure of around €500,000. Peter Urdl, Schwarzenegger’s childhood friend and a former mayor of Thal, played a central role in the museum initiative. The idea had been discussed for years before the project moved forward. Schwarzenegger supported the plan by providing personal belongings for display. The house was dedicated to its new purpose on his 64th birthday, July 30, 2011. It officially opened on October 7 that year with the unveiling of a large bronze statue outside the building.What visitors can see inside the museumThe Arnold Schwarzenegger Museum traces his life through childhood objects and memorabilia from his public career. Visitors can see his childhood bed and a recreation of the family kitchen. These exhibits help convey the basic conditions in which he grew up. The bodybuilding section documents his rise in competitive sport. Schwarzenegger won the Mr Olympia title seven times and became one of the most influential figures in modern bodybuilding. The film displays feature objects associated with his Hollywood career, including memorabilia connected with The Terminator. Other exhibits cover his political career as governor of California from 2003 to 2011. The collection has expanded since the museum opened, with additional material related to his military service and film roles. Outside, a large bronze statue commemorates his achievements and welcomes visitors to the site.From bodybuilding champion to Hollywood starSchwarzenegger first became internationally known through bodybuilding. His success in competitions helped him establish a reputation before he moved into acting. His seven Mr Olympia victories remain central to his sporting legacy. His breakthrough in cinema came with Conan the Barbarian in 1982. Two years later, The Terminator established him as a major action star. He went on to appear in films including Predator, Total Recall and Terminator 2: Judgment Day. His career later expanded into politics. Schwarzenegger served as California’s 38th governor from 2003 to 2011. He also became known for environmental advocacy and initiatives related to fitness and public health. The museum brings these achievements together under one roof. It shows how his career developed from his early ambitions in Austria into success across sport, cinema and public office.The museum’s place in Thal todayThe Arnold Schwarzenegger Museum remains a visitor attraction in Thal. Its location allows fans to explore the place where he spent his formative years rather than simply viewing objects in a conventional exhibition space. The museum offers information about his childhood and later achievements, with exhibits covering bodybuilding, acting and politics. Visitors can also explore the village and surrounding area that shaped his early life. The official museum provides audio guides in German, English and Hungarian, allowing visitors to learn more about the collection as they move through the building. For Thal, the residence connects local history with an internationally recognised public figure. For fans, it offers a chance to see the humble beginnings behind a career that crossed several worlds. The former police residence now preserves Schwarzenegger’s life story for future generations.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Florida to execute a prisoner who killed his cellmate in hopes of getting a death sentence
articles.summary: MIAMI — A Florida prisoner who claimed he killed his cellmate so he could be moved to death row is set to be executed Tuesday, nearly 18 years after the fatal attack.
articles.body: MIAMI — A Florida prisoner who claimed he killed his cellmate so he could be moved to death row is set to be executed Tuesday, nearly 18 years after the fatal attack. James Robertson, 63, pleaded guilty to first-degree murder and waived all appeals in the 2008 strangling of Frank Hart. Robertson is set to receive a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke starting at noon. Robertson was supposed to be one of two executions carried out by Florida on Tuesday, but Gov. Ron DeSantis withdrew a death warrant last week for William Lee Thompson. The Republican governor did not provide a reason for withdrawing Thompson’s death warrant but had temporarily stayed his execution last month pending a psychiatric evaluation. Records show that this is the first time DeSantis has withdrawn a death warrant, which does not technically change Thompson’s sentence. He will remain on death row, and a new death warrant could be signed for him in the future. Robertson’s execution comes at a time of escalating attention on the death penalty in the U.S. In Tennessee, Christa Pike survived an execution attempt two weeks ago despite receiving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. And last week, the Pentagon announced that the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan would be livestreamed. Robertson wanted to be on death row According to court records, Robertson was incarcerated at Charlotte Correctional Institution, north of Fort Myers, in December 2008 when he tied several socks together and strangled Hart while the other man slept. Robertson told investigators that the attack was unprovoked and that he killed his cellmate so that he would be sentenced to death, rather than having to live out his days in prison. Robertson was 17 years old when he went to prison in 1980 for burglary and assault. Years of convictions for escape, battery and weapons while in prison kept adding time to his total sentence. Hart was sent to prison in 2003 following a sexual battery conviction. Robertson pleaded guilty and waived a penalty phase, where a jury would recommend the death penalty or life in prison. A judge sentenced Robertson to death, and he later waived all post-conviction proceedings. Robertson reiterated his position during a hearing earlier this month, telling a judge that he understood his execution had been scheduled and that he didn’t want to make any final appeals to the Florida Supreme Court or U.S. Supreme Court. Death penalty opponents question its deterrent effect While proponents of the death penalty have long claimed that it is a deterrent, Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty released a statement saying that this case demonstrates the opposite. “Frank Hart deserved to be safe in state custody, and his loved ones deserve our compassion,” the group’s legal and policy director, Maria DeLiberato, said in the statement. “When someone commits murder to try to secure his own execution, we have to confront the conditions that contributed to that decision and the reality that the existence of the death penalty may have caused the very violence it purportedly prevents.” A rare reprieve leaves another Florida prisoner on death row Meanwhile, DeSantis is the third Florida governor to sign a death warrant for Thompson. Bob Graham and Bob Martinez both scheduled executions for Thompson in the 1980s, but years of appeals and stays allowed him to avoid the electric chair, the state’s method of execution at the time. The 74-year-old death row inmate was convicted of first-degree murder, kidnapping and sexual battery in the 1976 killing of 23-year-old Sally Ivester. Thompson will remain on Florida’s death row, and a new death warrant could be signed for him in the future. His attorneys have said he suffers from dementia, and his health is failing. They said he should be relocated to an adequate medical facility to get the care he needs. Only one other Florida inmate remains alive following a death warrant signed by DeSantis. James Dailey, 80, was scheduled to die in late 2019 for the murder of a 14-year-old girl, but a federal judge halted the execution as attorneys argued against his guilt. The stay was eventually lifted, but DeSantis didn’t sign a new death warrant. The state halted all executions during the COVID-19 pandemic and didn’t restart until 2023. Florida has the nation’s busiest death chamber DeSantis, who leaves office in January, oversaw 19 executions in 2025, more than any other Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Robertson would be the state’s 17th execution of 2026, with two more already scheduled, not counting Thompson. William Reaves, 77, is scheduled to be executed on Oct. 20, followed by Jesse Guardado, 64, on Nov. 5. Reaves was convicted of fatally shooting a deputy after dropping a gun in front of the law enforcement officer in 1986. Guardado was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004. If Robertson, Reaves and Guardado are all executed as planned, that would match the state’s 2025 total, with eight weeks remaining in 2026. DeSantis has made few public comments about the unprecedented number of executions but explained previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out. “I felt I owed it to them to make sure this ran very smoothly. If I honestly thought someone was innocent, I would not pull the trigger,” the governor said last year. A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. in 2025. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half the 30 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.

articles.title: ‘My son was killed’: France faces backlash over police firearms bill
articles.summary: As protests nationwide protests rage, activists warn proposed law could lead to more impunity.
articles.body:
Paris, France – Issam El Khalfaoui’s teenage son Souhail was shot and killed by a police officer in 2021 in Marseille.

“When my son was killed during a police traffic stop, we realised how difficult it was to bring the truth to light. The police and the justice system took different actions to cover up the evidence. We realised that this was a deeply systemic issue,” El Khalfaoui told Al Jazeera. “The IGPN [National Police] lost the video that captured my son’s murder. The witnesses were not interviewed, and the case file completely disappeared from the court. That is the reality.”

France has one of the highest numbers of fatal police shootings in Western Europe. At least 69 people were killed by police or gendarmerie officers in 2024, compared with 49 in 2023 and 50 in 2022.

Now, French police are again facing scrutiny, this time over their tactics during clashes in education protests. A 15-year-old lost a hand from a police stun grenade , and another officer threw a tear gas canister at close range, shattering a 14-year-old’s jaw and several teeth. The use of stun grenades has since been halted. Authorities say 700 police have also been injured.

The unrest comes as a controversial bill that would presume police officers acted in self-defence when using firearms faces a vote in the Senate.

Khalfaoui launched a petition against the draft law that received more than 700,000 signatures. The measure, which critics describe as a “licence to kill”, was approved by the National Assembly in July.

Several advocacy groups, including Stop State Violence (SAVE), the Human Rights League (LDH) and Amnesty International, as well as left-wing lawmakers, organised protests in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Toulouse, which drew nearly 50,000 people on September 20.

Under the proposed law, police officers and gendarmes would be presumed to have acted in self-defence if they used weapons in the line of duty, placing the burden of proof on the complainant.

For El Khalfaoui, who co-founded SAVE after his 19-year-old son’s death, passing the law would only increase the police’s strength.

“In France, there has been a seizure of power by police unions,” El Khalfaoui said. “There’s a militarisation of the police that has no equivalent in Europe, and resources have been allocated to the police to ensure the police’s loyalty to the government.”

The draft law could entrench a sense of impunity, El Khalfaoui noted.

“It will be impossible to refute this presumption of self-defence,” he said.

Bruno Bartocetti, a regional representative for the police union, told French news channel BFMTV the El Khalfaoui case was an act of “self-defence beyond any doubt” and said Souhail wanted to “start a fight”.

The judicial case was closed in December 2021, but reopened when the family’s attorney filed a complaint for “obstruction of the discovery of truth” after surveillance camera videos disappeared. A new judge was appointed in 2025, and the court’s investigation is ongoing.

Nathalie Tehio, president of France’s Human Rights League (LDH), also fears the bill “enables police impunity”.

“If there’s no investigation anymore, that means the police officer can no longer be held responsible for anything,” she told Al Jazeera. “France is a European leader in the number of people killed by the police.”

A 2017 law permitting police officers to wield firearms if a vehicle does not comply with a traffic stop has led to five times as many fatal shootings, according to researchers. At the time, the law had broad political support, although several left-wing politicians have opposed the recent draft bill and participated in protests.

“All parliamentary groups voted in favour of this law in 2017 by a very large majority. There was support across the political spectrum, from the left to the right and the far-right,” Sebastien Roche, a researcher at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS), specialising in police and democracy, told Al Jazeera.

After legislative elections in 2024, French President Emmanuel Macron’s party was unable to form an absolute majority to pass legislation without entering a coalition with other parties.

“Successive governments under Emmanuel Macron, especially during his second term, have adopted ideas from the far right,” Roche said.

With France’s presidential elections in six months, political parties are vying for electors, Roche noted.

“The competition is already under way, and in this competition, the right is trying to win over far-right voters because the right in France has lost a great deal of its political strength to the far-right in national and European elections,” he said.

When a police officer shot and killed 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk , a boy of Algerian descent, in 2023, riots spread across the country.

Discrimination leads to more traffic stops, said Roche, and ultimately people of colour are at more risk of violence.

“The way the police monitor people’s behaviour is unfavourable to non-white people,” he said, citing studies he conducted in Bouches-du-Rhone in the Marseille region. “The probability of being stopped (by the police) is more than 50 percent higher for people who are not white.”

In 2001, Omer Mas Capitolin was in a work meeting when a disturbance from a police intervention on the street outside shook the building. Mas Capitolin went downstairs to ask the officers to move, but the police entered the association and handcuffed Mas Capitolin.

“They used a chokehold and pinned me to the ground. I couldn’t breathe or speak,” Mas Capitolin told Al Jazeera.

He later founded the Community House for Supportive Development (MCDS), a grassroots non-profit against police violence and discrimination. In 2021, six NGOs, including MCDS filed a class action suit against the French government, alleging systemic racial discrimination in police identity checks.

“We can call these identity checks discriminatory, along with everything that goes with them, including the refusal to comply, contempt of authority, resistance, and, increasingly today, the issue of illegal and excessive fines imposed on young people,” Mas Capitolin said.

In October, 2023, France’s high court recognised racial profiling during police identity checks, a ruling described by Human Rights Watch (HRW) as “historic”. But the court did not order French authorities to take the “necessary measures to end this long-standing, abusive practice” as it handed down the verdict in the case filed by the six groups, HRW said.

Also in 2021, the French state was condemned for “gross negligence” in an identity check of three high school students in Saint-Denis, north of Paris. Last year, the European Court of Human Rights condemned France for racial profiling of Karim Touil.

Despite these rulings, “everything is moving in the opposite direction”, Mas Capitolin said. “France is dealing with kids using military-grade weapons. Police officers are over-equipped and over-armed. I’m devastated.”

articles.title: Pope Leo enters Rome hospital for operation to remove a lung nodule
articles.summary: VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV was admitted to Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Tuesday ahead of surgery later in the day to remove a lung nodule, an operation that experts say will determine whether the lesion is malignant and if other treatment is needed.
articles.body: VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV was admitted to Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Tuesday ahead of surgery later in the day to remove a lung nodule, an operation that experts say will determine whether the lesion is malignant and if other treatment is needed. Leo appeared in good spirits when he left the Vatican, waving at well-wishers from a lowered car window. After the quick drive from the Vatican to the hospital, the pope got out of the car, shook hands with the medical team and waved at a crowd waiting for him outside. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed later in the afternoon by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora. The 71-year-old American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the small, localized nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed. The surgery, which is usually performed under general anesthesia, will require a weeklong hospital stay and the Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo’s audiences through Oct. 20. In the Vatican, some pilgrims were worried, hopeful and a little disappointed. Yolanda Avella, 57, was among thousands of people hoping to see Leo on during the weekly General Audience Wednesday. “Well, it’s not what I wanted, but we know it’s for the best. It’s for his health. So, we’re okay with that,” Avella, from Tampa, Fla., said as she stood in St. Peter’s Square. “I am a little worried because it is a nodule in the lung. But I know he’s going to be okay.” Rev. Pius Mathew, who had organized the visit from Tampa, said he was disappointed that the group would miss seeing the pope but added that Leo’s health comes first. “We prayed and we did the Mass yesterday,” he said. “We prayed together for the pope, for the recovery and the good surgery” Leo is expected to recover in the hospital for at least a week, and his engagements and audiences have been cancelled through to Oct. 20. This may give the pope just the interval needed to make his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. The current itinerary for the trip is ambitious and the longest of his papacy to date, calling for Leo to clock just over 19,000 miles on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides, and a significant altitude change in Peru. A churchman who saw Leo on Monday, Tokyo Cardinal Kikuchi Tsutomu, said Leo told him he felt fine and decided to have the surgery immediately so that he wouldn’t have to alter his upcoming travel plans to Latin America. But the decision clearly came as a surprise: While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is currently undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office. The nodule was discovered during regular checks, the Vatican has said. Kikuchi, the Tokyo archbishop who is also head of the Vatican’s charitable federation Caritas Internationalis, said Leo told him he felt no different than usual and was looking ahead to the trip. “He has decided to undergo surgery soon in order to not change his plans for future overseas trips, so there is no need to worry, as it is not an emergency,” Kikuchi wrote on the Facebook page of the Tokyo archdiocese. Tuesday is believed to be the second hospitalization for Leo, who is known to be sporty and in good shape, with weekly tennis games and swimming. As a young missionary priest, he came down with typhoid fever in 1985, soon after arriving in Chulucanas, Peru. The illness and hospitalization were a cathartic moment for him to decide to stay in the poverty and discomfort of Peru after living in relative comfort in Rome — a decision that ultimately paved the way to his papacy, according to an interview Leo gave to Elise Ann Allen in 2025 for “Pope Leo XIV: The Biography.” According to the book, Leo said he prayed to God to let him die rather than suffer the “horrible” pain of the fever. “I was hooked up to an IV, and I said, ‘If this is your sense of humor, Lord, I think you could do a little better.’ “Obviously, I survived; I recovered, but it turned out to be a very significant moment for me, because it was like, ‘Well, you’ve already dealt with the illness; you already see what the needs are here — the order, the Augustinians, the church are telling you, ‘We need you here; go for it.’ I never looked back.”

articles.title: In 2010, Ben Affleck co-founded Eastern Congo Initiative; by 2024, programmes it supported were delivering over 100 million litres of clean water across 10 service zones in eastern Congo
articles.summary: Hollywood actor Ben Affleck co-founded the Eastern Congo Initiative (ECI) in 2010 to support locally led development in the Democratic Republic of Congo
articles.body: Hollywood actor Ben Affleck co-founded the Eastern Congo Initiative (ECI) in 2010 to support locally led development in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). By 2024, initiatives supported by the organisation were delivering more than 100 million litres of clean water across 10 service zones in eastern Congo, according to ECI's official website. The organisation also reported that its supported initiatives enabled more than 400,000 people to access essential health services that year, highlighting the scale of its work beyond emergency aid.Founded by Affleck and social entrepreneur Whitney Williams, ECI focuses on supporting Congolese communities and organisations working to improve access to essential services, strengthen livelihoods and advance justice. Rather than relying exclusively on externally designed aid programmes, it says its approach centres on local leadership and partnerships with community-based organisations.The clean-water figures reflect the role of Asili, a social enterprise that provides water and healthcare services in South Kivu province. ECI acquired Asili in 2020, building on an initiative designed to make essential services more accessible and financially sustainable for local communities.From Hollywood activism to community-led developmentAffleck's involvement in eastern Congo began with visits that exposed him to the resilience of communities living amid conflict and persistent development challenges. According to ECI, these experiences helped inspire the organisation's establishment in 2010.ECI describes itself as the first US-based organisation dedicated exclusively to supporting communities in eastern Congo through advocacy and grant-making. Its work includes funding local organisations and backing initiatives intended to strengthen economic opportunities and access to essential services.Williams co-founded the organisation with Affleck and has served as its vice chair. The organisation's model emphasises working alongside Congolese leaders rather than treating communities solely as recipients of international assistance. Over the years, its work has expanded across several areas, including agriculture, social enterprise, healthcare and justice. Asili became one of its flagship initiatives, bringing water services and primary healthcare closer to communities that often face difficulties accessing reliable infrastructure.Asili: a water network designed around local needsAsili, whose name means “foundation” in Swahili, was developed as a social enterprise to provide essential services through a locally operated model. Its origins date to a 2013 human-centred design process led by IDEO.org and funded by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), with the American Refugee Committee, now known as Alight, serving as an incubating partner.Local women were involved in shaping the enterprise from its early stages. According to Virridy Carbon's overview of the water network, seven Congolese mothers participated in the design process, contributing to decisions ranging from the business plan to the organisation's identity.Asili was launched in South Kivu in 2014. ECI acquired it in August 2020, and it now operates as an independently registered local organisation. Its approach combines water access, primary healthcare and other community services rather than treating clean water as a stand-alone intervention.The model is intended to provide communities with a more consistent source of essential services. Its water stations are operated by locally employed women known as “Water Mamas”, who manage water sales and interact with customers. Virridy reports that the network also employs skilled plumbers to maintain the infrastructure.100 million litres of water delivered in 2024ECI's reported 2024 figures offer an indication of the scale of the programme. According to the organisation's official impact page, its supported initiatives delivered more than 100 million litres of clean water across 10 service zones during the year.Virridy's overview provides further details about the network's infrastructure, reporting 69 water stations across South Kivu, 84 Water Mamas and 27 skilled plumbers. It also records approximately 60 kilometres of pipeline installed since the network was established.The two organisations report water volumes using different measures. ECI's figure refers specifically to delivery during 2024, while Virridy lists 414 million litres as the network's cumulative total in its 2024 overview. These figures should not be treated as competing estimates of the same period.The system's locally operated structure is another important part of the initiative. Water Mamas earn income through their work at the stations, while maintenance staff help keep the network functioning. The arrangement links access to clean water with local employment, allowing residents to participate in the service's day-to-day operation.Clean water during displacement and conflictThe programme's importance became particularly visible during the displacement crisis in eastern Congo. In 2024, fighting forced people from their homes, placing additional pressure on communities and basic services in areas receiving displaced families.In a November 27, 2024, update published on GlobalGiving, ECI described its response in Minova, an agricultural and fishing village in eastern DRC. The organisation said it had installed two piped-water systems serving major host areas and extended its network to provide water to displaced families.The initiative also distributed more than 3,000 jerry cans to help households collect and store water. Its local water point remained open daily, while healthcare teams provided medical assistance to displaced people and host communities.A subsequent report published on March 25, 2025, said a 400,000-litre reservoir in Minova had supplied more than 18 million litres of water between June and November 2024. The report described the reservoir as an important resource for residents and displaced people, with the network also extended to two major displacement camps.The response continued into 2025. In a report dated July 31, 2025, ECI said it had distributed more than 11.1 million litres of safe drinking water between January and June alone. Since the previous June, it reported that more than 30 million litres had reached displaced people and local residents.These figures relate to the specific emergency response in Minova, not the entire Asili network. They nevertheless illustrate how local water infrastructure can support communities during periods of heightened need.A longer-term approach to essential servicesECI's work in eastern Congo extends beyond water delivery. The organisation says its supported initiatives enabled more than 400,000 people to access essential health services in 2024, alongside the clean-water programme. Its approach reflects an effort to connect humanitarian needs with longer-term development by supporting locally led organisations and infrastructure. Asili's water stations, healthcare facilities and locally employed operators form part of that strategy.The model does not remove the wider challenges facing eastern Congo, where conflict and displacement continue to disrupt access to essential services. But the reported water-delivery figures demonstrate the reach of a network designed to operate within local communities.For Affleck and Williams, the initiative they founded in 2010 has developed into a broader effort to support Congolese-led solutions. By 2024, the clean-water programme had reached a scale exceeding 100 million litres delivered in a year across 10 service zones, while its emergency response in Minova showed how the infrastructure could also be used to assist displaced families.You use AI every day. articles.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine received no intelligence from partners on incoming missile strike on Kyiv
articles.summary: Ukraine received no early warning from its partners about a Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv in which five missiles hit civilian infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday in a post on X. Zelenskyy characterized the barrage on the capital as “particularly vile,” and emphasized that receiving intelligence from Ukraine’s partners on such ballistic missile attacks “helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues.”
articles.body: Ukraine received no early warning from its partners about a Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv in which five missiles hit civilian infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday in a post on X. Zelenskyy characterized the barrage on the capital as “particularly vile,” and emphasized that receiving intelligence from Ukraine’s partners on such ballistic missile attacks “helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues.” “This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed — when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he wrote. He did not apportion blame for the lack of warning. Russia’s war in Ukraine hasn’t seen major shifts on the ground since last year, but Ukraine is struggling to fend off Moscow’s intensified aerial attacks on cities that include speedy ballistic missiles and high-flying jet-powered drones. Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 100 weapons since Monday evening. Among the damage was a residential building in the northeastern city of Kharkiv that was destroyed, killing four people despite an all-night rescue operation, he said. Russia has increasingly used attacks on civilian infrastructure such as energy facilities to deny Ukrainians power, heat and running water during the 4 1/2-year war, hoping to wear down public support for Ukraine’s response to Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Ukraine, meanwhile, has launched strikes against Russian energy sites like oil refineries, sometimes deep within Russian territory, despite requests by the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump to refrain from doing so. Trump has blamed Zelenskyy for record U.S. diesel prices — rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran — and struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday to import diesel from Russia in an attempt to bring fuel prices down ahead of U.S. midterm elections. Meanwhile, Trump claimed on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed on an “energy ceasefire” in which both parties would refrain from striking each other’s energy infrastructure. Russia has not confirmed the existence of such a deal, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Tuesday saying only that “contacts on this matter continue.” Zelenskyy on Tuesday said Ukraine had not struck Russian oil refineries or other energy sites in the two days since Trump announced the purported deal. He criticized Moscow for what he said were Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities and critical infrastructure in the time since Trump’s announcement. “These are absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said. The claim that Ukraine has halted its strikes on energy sites could not be independently verified, but neither Russian officials nor media have reported Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries since the energy truce was announced. Russian strikes across Ukraine caused injuries and deaths overnight Monday and into Tuesday, with Zelenskyy saying that in addition to the four deaths in the apartment building in Kharkiv, 41 people were wounded in the city in one evening alone. A woman was wounded in a Russian strike on a private home in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district, the Kyiv city military administration said, while a Russian drone hit a residential building in the village of Murovane, near the western city of Lviv, during a morning attack Tuesday, Lviv Mayor Andrii Sadovyi said. One person was killed in the Fastiv district of the Kyiv region and at least two others were hurt in a Russian attack on the area, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration. A Russian drone struck an educational institution in the center of Rivne in northwest Ukraine, wounding 14 people, according to Oleksandr Koval, head of the Rivne regional military administration. The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement Tuesday that its forces overnight “launched coordinated strikes using ground-based precision weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles against Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, logistics centers, railway and port infrastructure, as well as vessels involved in delivering military cargo to Ukraine.” The ministry also said a bulk carrier headed to the port of Mykolaiv with military cargo on board was hit in the estuary of the Dnipro and Bug rivers along the Black Sea. The Russian Defense Ministry on Tuesday said its air defenses overnight shot down 604 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions and the Sea of Azov. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 417 drones targeted the Moscow region. Most were downed far away, while 65 were intercepted as they approached the Russian capital. A school, two private houses and a car were damaged in the attack in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow, Gov. Vladislav Shapsha said.

articles.title: BA flight forced to turn back to Gatwick over cracked window
articles.summary: British Airways said the plane landed safely at Gatwick and passengers were due to resume their journey.
articles.body:
A British Airways flight en route to Portugal was forced to return to Gatwick Airport on Tuesday due to a minor technical issue, reported to be a cracked window.

Flight BA2660 was heading to Faro in the Algarve but diverted over north-western France in order to return to London Gatwick.

AirNav Radar, a flight data provider, posted on X that "a passenger window is cracked. Flight deck going through checks before deciding were to divert".

A spokesperson for British Airways said the plane landed safely at Gatwick due to a "minor technical issue" and passengers were due to resume their journey.

"We have apologised to customers for the delay to their journey, and our teams are working hard to get their travel plans back on track," they said.

Airnav Radar reported that the BA Airbus A321 squawked the 7700 emergency code, which is used when there are mechanical or technical problems on board aircraft.

Last week, a BA flight bound for Chicago spent five hours circling over Ireland, before turning back and landing at London Heathrow, where it had taken off.

The flight issued an emergency alert and passengers reported oxygen masks dropped in the cabin, as well as turbulence. Tracking data showed it rapidly descended from 37,000 feet to 9,000 feet.

And in August Serbian national Ljubisa Karović's head and right shoulder were sucked out of the window on a Ryanair flight, leaving him "seriously injured and in shock".

Ryanair subsequently said the window may have been damaged by a foreign object.

articles.title: MI5 tackling more state threats than during Cold War, warns intelligence chief
articles.summary: Sir Ken McCallum says operations to tackle terrorism and state threats are now roughly of an "equal scale".
articles.body:
MI5 is devoting more resource to countering state threats than during the Cold War, the head of the intelligence service has said.

Sir Ken McCallum said threats from foreign adversaries had quadrupled in the last decade, with Russia "aggressor number one" as well as increased Iran-linked aggression against Jewish sites and military bases.

At an annual speech in London, MI5's chief said Russia was waging hybrid warfare at a time when AI was "supercharging the cyber-security contest between attackers and defenders".

He also warned of rising threats from "extreme right-wing terrorism" and said MI5 had "caught terrorists seeking to exploit Al," including by integrating the technology with drones.

He said the biggest threat from the misuse of AI was extremist groups using the technology to harness new and existing bioweapons.

However, he noted that work countering terrorism and state threats was now "pretty much of equal scale" which he described as a "huge shift" in recent years.

Sir Ken said Russia had stopped short of "conventional conflict" against Nato and is instead trying to unsettle European countries while its progress in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine is "minimal and horrifically costly".

Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.

These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.

Sir Ken said MI5 successes in identifying and expelling Russian spies from the UK had left the Kremlin dependent on paying proxies for attempted attacks.

"With its traditional covert footprint eviscerated by almost 1,000 expulsions since the invasion, the Kremlin's global toolkit is weak, he said.

"So we see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding."

He added: "These are not the actions of a great power with the strategic upper hand."

His comments come as a growing number of leaders across Europe have warned Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.

Asked after the speech about Prime Minister Andy Burnham's recent comments that Russia interfered with the Brexit referendum , Sir Ken said it was "not new news" that there had been attempts from Moscow but distinguished between "interference attempted" and "outcome achieved".

He said it was a matter of public record that there were pieces in Russian media and "so-called internet trolls and bot farms" seeking to influence the Brexit debate, but also stressed that the result of the 2016 referendum was "not in dispute".

He added that he was "worried" about the the ongoing debate on Russian interference.

"I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall," he told reporters.

Meanwhile, Sir Ken warned that Iran is also expanding a hybrid campaign in the UK.

The intelligence chief said there had been 50 arrests in the last year over Iran-linked activities.

Much of this Iranian aggression has been aimed at Jewish communities, Sir Ken added, and also at "harder targets, like military sites".

Sir Ken did not mention arrests at RAF Fairford directly during his speech, but told reporters afterwards the incident was "not unique".

He added: "We have seen Iranian interest beyond RAF Fairford in the UK."

The incident at the airbase in Gloucesteshire, where three suspicious vans were seen parked nearby, has seen seven people arrested and bailed by counter-terrorism police.

Burnham has said the incident was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard".

The MI5 head said in his speech: "What I can say is that those who seek to cause mayhem on British streets - whether hired thugs here or their paymasters overseas - will meet an unflinching response."

Sir Ken added that the National Security Act - a 2023 law designed to target people working against UK interests for foreign powers - is in heavy use, and has been employed to tackle threats from China as well as Iran and Russia.

On the emerging threat posed by AI, Sir Ken said: "It can produce propaganda and radicalising material tailored to the individual.

"We've caught terrorists seeking to exploit Al to improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies, with Al-enabled drones adding a new twist."

Sir Ken said the bioweapons threat posed by AI was "not yet realised" but warned the technology has the "potential to change the stakes".

"These risks are real. The UK Intelligence Community - MI5, GCHQ, MI6 - is working closely with the UK's globally respected AI Security Institute to take them on."

Sir Ken said AI poses unknown threats, telling Thames House: "Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are".

He announced MI5 had launched an AI Threat Assessment Centre, which he said would assess sources and "separate the bluster from the realities".

In April, the UK's terrorism threat level was raised to severe for the first time in five years, meaning an attack is highly likely.

Sir Ken said Islamist groups like Al Qaeda and so-called Islamic State both continue to direct and inspire attacks, while the increased risk was also driven "in significant part" by extreme right-wing terrorism.

He continued: "Over the last year the most marked trend has been an increase in cases where extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent."

Sir Ken said extreme right-wing terrorism tended to "skew young", driven by the internet - adding that MI5 had in recent months investigated a "radicalised extreme right-wing 13-year-old here in the UK".

He said: "That investigation generated insight that enabled one of our international partners to prevent a lethal attack on their soil."

articles.title: Fiery discovery may finally unravel 2,000-year-old mystery involving Julius Caesar
articles.summary: A 66-foot stone-and-timber wall found near Notre Dame may belong to Lutetia, the ancient Gallic city described by Julius Caesar in his writings. The French Ministry of Culture announced the find.
articles.body: Archaeologists in Paris recently unearthed an ancient wall that may belong to a long-lost city — potentially solving a centuries-old mystery dating back to the times of Julius Caesar. The discovery was recently announced by the French Ministry of Culture. In a translated statement, officials said a wall discovered in the courtyard of the Hôtel-Dieu hospital — just a stone's throw away from Notre Dame Cathedral in the city's 4th arrondissement — might have belonged to the ancient city of Lutetia. 'DIG OF THE CENTURY' BENEATH NOTRE DAME REVEALS MYSTERIOUS MARKINGS, ANCIENT SECRETS The excavation, which began in February, was conducted ahead of a "major redevelopment project," officials said. "Researchers initially expected to uncover traces of ancient dwellings, roads, or settlements dating to the medieval and early modern periods," the translated statement read. "Instead, alongside those remains, they discovered a stone-and-timber wall characteristic of ancient Gallic fortifications." The settlement was mentioned by Julius Caesar in his writings, particularly "The Gallic Wars" — but no conclusive archaeological evidence confirmed its location until now. ANCIENT CLUE CRACKS OPEN A 2,000-YEAR-OLD MYSTERY NEAR FAMED COLOSSEUM In a statement, French Culture Minister Catherine Pégard said officials "may be looking at one of the most important discoveries ever made in understanding Gallic Lutetia. "Scientific caution still requires us to verify its function and chronology, but the convergence of evidence is particularly remarkable," added Pégard. Photos from the excavation show large, weathered stone blocks stacked in uneven rows. The wall, which stretches roughly 66 feet, bears evidence of a major fire, while radiocarbon testing of wooden elements found at the site suggests they date to between 200 B.C. and 10 B.C. GRISLY DISCOVERY FROM LEGENDARY ROMAN EMPEROR'S REIGN REVEALS SOLDIERS' REMAINS, WEAPONS Researchers believe the structure may have served as a defensive fortification for the Gauls. The wall's stonework showed signs of fire damage, while archaeologists also uncovered burned seeds and the remains of a charred wooden building nearby. Caesar's account indicated the Gallic Parisii tribe burned its own fortified settlement in 52 B.C. to prevent it from falling into Roman hands. "Today, with this wall and its archaeological context, we may finally hold the key to solving the mystery." "The architecture of the wall, with its large stone blocks and system of interlocking wooden beams, very quickly made us think of a wall built in the Gallic tradition," she said in the statement. Due to the redevelopment project, the ancient wall cannot remain at its original location, officials said. Looking ahead, researchers plan to conduct further excavations to determine the wall's age and purpose. Stéphane Deschamps, regional archaeological conservator at the DRAC Île-de-France, said that the discovery "fills a gap in the archaeological record." articles.title: Spanish royals make rare visit to Ceuta after migrant crisis
articles.summary: Spain's exclave in North Africa is still dealing with the aftermath of an influx of 70,000 people from Morocco in July.
articles.body:
King Felipe VI has begun a visit to Ceuta as the Spanish exclave continues to grapple with a migrant crisis triggered by an influx of around 70,000 people from Morocco in July.

It marks the first Spanish royal visit to the city in nearly two decades and comes amid tensions with Morocco, which maintains a longstanding claim to the territory.

The majority of migrants have left since the surge across its border, during which humanitarian organisations estimate at least 141 people died. But thousands have remained, mostly sleeping rough until recently.

The situation has sparked concern locally and criticism of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's response ahead of elections next month, with immigration set to be a key issue.

The king and Queen Letizia were greeted by cheering crowds waving Spanish flags as they visited Ceuta's city hall upon their arrival on Tuesday, where they met local officials to hear how the crisis had affected the territory.

The pair said the visit - the first since that taken by King Felipe's father, Juan Carlos I, in 2007 - had been "long awaited and long overdue" in a message in the city's book of honour, broadcaster RTVE reported.

They added they aimed to demonstrate "the commitment of the entire country to the future of the people of Ceuta, which is the future of Spain".

The royal couple will later attend an interfaith ceremony at the Sidi Embarek Muslim cemetery where many of those who died during the summer's crossings were buried.

King Felipe is due to deliver a speech from Ceuta's Parador hotel in the evening, before travelling on Wednesday to Melilla - Spain's other city on the North African coast, which Morocco also claims.

The Spanish government meanwhile said the "historic" visit marked a turning point in the crisis. Asked whether they feared how Morocco might respond, a spokeswoman said it was also "absolutely normal" for the royal family to visit "two Spanish cities".

The king and queen were handed the key to the city by Ceuta's conservative Mayor Juan Jesús Vivas, who said the influx had turned the exclave into "a pressure cooker that could explode at any moment", placing social cohesion, essential services and security at risk.

He had previously described the situation as "the most serious national security crisis of the democratic era" in Spain, and estimated that 15,000 migrants remained in the city.

Central government estimates are much lower, with officials saying 7,400 places were available to house the migrants.

Since the crossing in late July, residents of the 18.5 sq km (7.2 sq miles) territory have expressed concerns about safety and pressure on local infrastructure. Some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.

The majority of arrivals had been sleeping rough on Ceuta's beaches until the central government erected makeshift shelters last month, as part of its efforts to identify the migrants and determine whether they were eligible to remain in the city.

The crisis thrust Ceuta and immigration to the centre of the national political arena, prompting demonstrations on mainland Spain in support of Ceuta's people and criticism of the Socialist-led government's handling of the situation.

It has also thrown a spotlight on Spain's relationship with Morocco, who many initially blamed for the situation - although Sánchez has maintained there is no proof that Spain's neighbour knowingly allowed or engineered the mass crossing.

Earlier this week, he confirmed a media report that Moroccan military vessels had entered Spanish waters off Ceuta during the crossing, but played down the importance of the incident.

Spanish intelligence warned of Ceuta mass crossing plans before surge

Protests in Spain against government's handling of Ceuta migrant crisis

Morocco has meanwhile reiterated its longstanding sovereignty claims to both Ceuta and Melilla amid the crisis.

In August, its Justice Minister Abdellatif Ouahbi spoke of his country's "historical and geographical right" to the exclaves and called for bilateral talks on the issue, which the Spanish government rejected.

The opposition has accused Sánchez of failing to stand up to Rabat. The leader of the conservative People's Party (PP), Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said Sánchez was lying about the causes of the crossing and was guilty of "frivolity" on this issue.

"To Morocco, [we should offer] loyalty and good neighbourliness, but also firmness," he said.

articles.title: African Union holds Kigali talks as fighting continues in eastern DRC
articles.summary: Three former African presidents discussed security commitments, refugee protection and regional cooperation.
articles.body:
Kigali, Rwanda – The African Union (AU) has held consultations in Kigali, Rwanda, as part of efforts to advance the peace process in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where fighting continues despite diplomatic initiatives to end the conflict.

The consultations, held on October 6, focused on implementing the Washington Peace Agreement, security arrangements, the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration of fighters, refugee protection and regional economic cooperation, the AU said in a statement.

The delegation comprised former Ethiopian President Sahle-Work Zewde, former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta and former Botswana President Mokgweetsi Masisi. Zewde is the deputy chairperson of the AU Panel of Facilitators for the eastern DRC peace process.

The Kigali consultations followed meetings in Goma, eastern DRC, on October 5. According to the AU, the delegation met representatives of the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+) and the Alliance Fleuve Congo/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23).

Following the Goma meetings, the AU panel called for respect for ceasefire commitments, cooperation with verification mechanisms and restraint from actions that could undermine the peace process. It also stressed the need to protect civilians, ensure safe humanitarian access and prevent sexual and gender-based violence.

In Kigali, the facilitators held separate consultations with Rwandan officials and representatives of regional institutions. The AU said the discussions covered security commitments, the protection of refugees and returnees, and regional economic cooperation, including mineral traceability, cross-border trade, energy and infrastructure.

The facilitators said they would continue their engagements in Kinshasa as part of efforts to support dialogue and advance the peace process.

The consultations come amid parallel diplomatic efforts to address the conflict. The Washington Peace Agreement, signed by the DRC and Rwanda on June 27, 2025, includes security commitments intended to address concerns over armed groups and the presence of forces in eastern DRC.

Implementation remains a central issue. At a meeting of the agreement’s Joint Oversight Committee in June 2026, the parties expressed concern over escalating fighting and called for the agreement to be fully implemented, including commitments concerning the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) and the disengagement of forces.

The Washington agreement is separate from the Doha Framework for a Comprehensive Peace Agreement, signed on November 15, 2025, by representatives of the Congolese government and AFC/M23 under Qatar’s mediation.

The Doha framework provides a basis for negotiations between the two sides on outstanding issues, including security arrangements and ceasefire monitoring. Subsequent discussions have focused on implementing existing commitments and negotiating remaining protocols.

The two processes address different aspects of the conflict: the Washington agreement deals with relations and security commitments between the DRC and Rwanda, while the Doha process addresses negotiations between the Congolese government and AFC/M23.

Kinshasa accuses Rwanda of supporting AFC/M23, an allegation Kigali denies. Rwanda, in turn, accuses the Congolese government of supporting and arming the FDLR, which it considers a threat to its national security.

The Washington agreement includes commitments by the DRC to address the FDLR and by Rwanda concerning the disengagement of its forces and the lifting of defensive measures. The parties have continued to discuss how those commitments will be implemented and verified.

The continued diplomatic engagement reflects the challenges facing efforts to resolve the conflict, with security commitments and negotiations involving different parties proceeding on separate tracks.

The AU’s consultations in Goma and Kigali form part of its wider mediation efforts. Whether those efforts contribute to improved security will depend on the implementation of commitments by the parties and continued engagement in the respective peace processes.

articles.title: Joe Cordina was 'retaliating' when he punched man to ground - court
articles.summary: Joe Cordina is on trial charged with two counts of assault by beating after a fight on 27 February.
articles.body:
Former boxing world champion Joe Cordina was "retaliating" during a fight where he punched a man at a petrol station, a court has heard.

Cordina is standing trial charged with assault by beating relating to an incident on 27 February involving Jamie O'Brien, who previously admitted a charge of assault by beating . A second assault by beating charge against Cordina was dropped on Tuesday.

Cardiff Magistrates' Court heard the altercation came to light days later, after a video was published on Wales Online, filmed by a witness at a Texaco garage in the Pentwyn area of Cardiff.

O'Brien's sister told police her brother "hated" Cordina, the court was told, and she feared he had "sought out" Cordina.

CCTV footage of the incident "which took place over several minutes" was played to the court, showing Cordina filling up his car and walking over to O'Brien who stood on the pavement nearby.

Prosecutor Alex Orndal said O'Brien "pushed Mr Cordina with his shoulder" and Cordina then "punched him with sufficient force to push him to the ground", where he then pushed him "repeatedly".

"Mr Cordina has initiated the confrontation," Orndal said, adding "Cordina was not protecting himself but retaliating".

There was then "aggression" from O'Brien, the court heard, as Cordina raised a golf club and O'Brien lunged at him, before a number of blows were exchanged.

O'Brien was eventually restrained and "posed no further threat", the court heard, but Cordina then threw a further punch at him.

In a police interview, Cordina denied the alleged offence, saying that "having been shoved" he "felt threatened" and then punched him later "out of instinct" due to O'Brien's actions.

Cordina's defence barrister, Tom Crowther, told the court O'Brien had been identified by family members from the video circulating online, who had raised concerns about his behaviour.

Tom Crowther KC, defending, asked investigating officer PC Samuel Penman to watch the video that had circulated online.

He said it was plain to see that they were "watching and waiting" for Cordina, suggesting it was a set up.

Penman said it was not obvious but he did agree that the person filming "seemingly started recording prior to any physical altercation going on".

The court heard that, when O'Brien was arrested, he "argued with officers" and "challenged" them.

Penman admitted it was a "mistake" not to question O'Brien's sister about her concerns that her brother held a "vendetta" against Cordina.

articles.title: Iran sees ‘false flag’ operations after UK blames IRGC for airbase incident
articles.summary: Iran has been accused of being behind a plot against an airbase in the UK.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has condemned the United Kingdom’s attribution of an alleged plot near a military airbase in the town of Fairford to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which it views as part of a greater Western effort.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Parliament on Monday that the suspected plot last month against the Royal Air Force base was “highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran” and “almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard”.

Burnham promised action against what he described as Iran-linked “criminal networks” and their financing networks.

The UK announced sanctions against two Iranian nationals over alleged “hostile activity” at RAF Fairford in southern England.

It follows an incident around the base, which hosted US military aircraft, in the early hours of September 27, when five British men in their 20s suspected of “terrorism” and explosives offences were arrested. The men were not charged and were released on police bail. Another two men were also arrested and later released.

Information about a suspected security threat to RAF Fairford and the events remains opaque.

In a statement late Monday, the Iranian ministry described the UK’s claims of an Iranian role as “an ugly plot” that would also serve to “evade accountability for Britain’s participation” in the ongoing war against Iran on February 28.

It said the UK had failed to provide sufficient evidence to back its claims and rejected the accusations of Iranian involvement as a “clumsy false flag operation”.

“Britain’s track record of fabricating security claims against other countries, which have in some cases led to damaging tensions and conflicts in West Asia, is well known,” the ministry said, without elaborating.

British Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said investigators assessed the coordinator to be a known individual based in Iran, although she did not name that person or disclose the supporting communications, financial records or other intelligence.

RAF Fairford is a prominent base for United States aircraft that have participated in the war on Iran, which began on February 28 following US and Israeli strikes that killed several Iranian leaders and officials, including Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

After news of the incident, the US withdrew approximately a dozen B-1 bombers from the Fairford base.

US media cited unnamed sources as alleging there was intelligence suggesting the bombers could run the risk of being hit by small drone attacks.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu publicly claimed at the start of October that his administration warned the UK about a plot.

“We gave the Brits the intel that there was going to be an attack, and it’s an Iranian-sponsored attack, and pretty much the next day they slapped sanctions on us,” he said during an interview with US broadcaster Fox News.

Netanyahu was criticising UK measures in response to the illegal expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank amid a diplomatic dispute.

Earlier this month, Tehran grouped the Fairford incident with allegations surrounding the Flydubai cockpit attack – which authorities in the United Arab Emirates claimed was a “suicide” mission to crash the plane at Israel’s Ben Gurion airport in Tel Aviv.

“I think even a schoolchild recognised how amateurishly it was designed,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said about the aircraft incident.

He also argued that such incidents were being manufactured to assign blame and justify a war facing public opposition in the US and elsewhere.

IRNA, the official news website of the Iranian government, argued in an analysis last week that the Western-led vote at the board of governors of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to refer the case of Iran’s nuclear programme to the United Nations Security Council could be classified as another attempt to pressure Iran to capitulate to US demands.

It said increasing reports over recent weeks attributing a major role and responsibility to Tehran for the considerable battlefield advances gained by the Houthis in Yemen pointed to a “plan to identify Iran as the main reason for insecurity” on the regional and global stage.

“The series of suspicious incidents recently, which have been attributed to Iran by the US president and senior officials without offering any evidence, appear to be a coordinated wave to smear Iran,” IRNA said.

But UK officials have advanced undeterred with measures against Iran in reaction to the Fairford incident.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband summoned Iran’s ambassador and sanctioned one person identified as an IRGC counterespionage chief, and another described as a facilitator for a criminal network. Measures included asset freezes and travel bans. But the two named men were not explicitly identified as Fairford’s organisers.

The UK government in July designated the IRGC as a “terrorist” organisation.

On Friday, the UK was among 32 countries, including Australia, Canada, France, Germany, and the US, to “condemn in the strongest terms Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyberattacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners”.

“We recognise the United Kingdom’s attribution of Iran’s involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford on 27 September. The UK has also concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors,” they said in a joint statement.

Armed police maintain road blocks and security checks around RAF Fairford on September 28, 2026 in Fairford, UK [Leon Neal/Getty Images]

articles.title: Trump’s diesel deal opens a new rift with Europe over Ukraine
articles.summary: Trump calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced, while Europe devotes summit to funding Ukraine.
articles.body:
Russia has claimed it can supply even more diesel to the global market than the quantities agreed with United States President Donald Trump.

“By the end of the year, we could reach supply volumes of 3.5 million tonnes per month to global markets, just as was the case before the crisis,” Alexander Novak, Russian deputy prime minister, told the news programme Vesti on Monday.

President Vladimir Putin and Trump spoke on Friday on an agreement expected to bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel to global markets in October, half a million tonnes in November, and a million tonnes in December.

“Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump posted.

But experts are sceptical, and the move has opened a rift between the US and Europe on the Ukraine war.

Kostis Stambolis, executive director of the Institute of Energy for South-East Europe (IENE), described the US move as “purely political” and designed to put Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a corner.

Trump wants to signal that the US has “no problem with Russia”, unlike Europe, he said.

“Russia produces 5.8 million tonnes of diesel a month. Two million are likely to be available for export,” he added.

Europe has reacted to the diesel deal by backing Ukraine, whose war funding will be “front and centre” of this week’s European Council summit, European Commission President Ursula Von Der Leyen said on Sunday.

Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen on Monday called on Europeans to ban all tourist visas to Russians.

Stambolis believes Trump was leveraging European weakness to shift its position on Ukraine.

“About 30 European refineries have closed in the past 15 years for environmental reasons, because they have to pay to emit greenhouse gases,” he said, referring to Europe’s Emissions Trading Scheme, “so now Europe is not self-sufficient in products”.

Trump is showing the Europeans “he doesn’t want to deal with Europe and to hell with them … This is opening the rift between the US and the EU further,” said Stambolis.

Ukraine says it has destroyed roughly half of Russia’s refining capacity, forcing Moscow to stop exporting lucrative petroleum products which help it to finance its war.

It has also bombed Russian tankers carrying crude oil to global markets.

Zelenskyy said the strategy was effective, and Trump’s deal, which would suspend sanctions on Russian oil products until April 2027, undermined it.

“Gifts to Putin will not lead to peace,” Zelenskyy said Saturday. “Any weakening of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious sign of weakness.”

Although Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday, leading Ukraine to suspend its attacks on refineries, Russian strikes pounded Kyiv’s energy grid and killed 12 people in Dnipropetrovsk.

“I do not think he has earned a respite,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said of Zelenskyy.

Europe supports Ukraine’s economic strategy against Russia’s war machine, but Trump has blamed it for raising petrol prices at the pump for Americans as he heads into Congressional midterm elections in early November.

“[Zelenskyy] wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world,” Trump told reporters in the White House after Zelenskyy’s reaction.

“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president ,” he said.

Trump has followed a seemingly self-contradictory policy towards Russia.

He cut US military aid to Ukraine when he assumed power in January 2025, but agreed to sell Europe weapons to help Ukraine.

He had a public dispute with Zelenskyy in the Oval Office in February 2025, saying “You don’t have the cards,” but at the NATO summit this year said Zelenskyy had “done an amazing job” and “been very effective”.

Last month, Trump signed the Lindsey Graham Act, which would allow him to punish countries buying Russian oil. Eleven days later, he reversed policy.

“The moment the pendulum comes to one side, Trump tries to balance it with a completely different and opposite tool,” said Victoria Vdovychenko, an expert on European security at Cambridge University’s Centre for Geopolitics.

“In this way he sees how he controls the narrative, but also negotiations of any kind,” she told Al Jazeera. “So this pendulum will continue to prevail.”

According to the US Energy Information Agency (EIA), average US diesel and petrol prices briefly spiked but ultimately changed little on account of the Ukraine war, yet they have risen a great deal on account of the US-Israel war on Iran.

US diesel was priced at $4.10 a gallon on the day of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, February 24, 2022. It had fallen to $3.81 on the eve of Trump’s Gulf war, February 28, 2026.

It has since risen by 78 percent, to $6.19 in early October.

It is a similar story for US regular unleaded gasoline, priced at $3.48 a gallon before the Russian invasion. It stood at $2.79 before Trump’s Gulf war, but has since risen by half, to $4.15 a gallon.

The US government has little room to reduce taxes, which constitute just 11 or 12 percent of retail price, so it can only manipulate prices through supply.

“If the market knows that there will be much more diesel in the coming weeks, it factors this into today’s prices and discounts it now,” Stambolis told Al Jazeera.

But much more important in bringing down oil prices than the Trump-Putin deal will be an October 2 announcement by the G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil from strategic reserves, he said.

A remainder of 80 million barrels from a previous, 400-million-tonne release in March will also be released.

“This release will start happening in the next two weeks,” Stambolis said. “The world is 5 million barrels a day short of crude compared to before the Gulf war. It’s a very significant percentage on 100 million. All prices vary on this margin.”
