articles.title: Is Zelensky right to say data centre strikes have taken down Russian bots?
articles.summary: Experts say there is no evidence that Russian trolls have been affected by Ukraine’s Yandex attacks.
articles.body:
Claims that Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centres reduced Kremlin-linked bot networks have spread widely online, but experts have told BBC Verify there is no evidence the attacks have significantly reduced them.

Viral social media posts have claimed there has been a significant drop in influence operations in recent days, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky suggesting on Monday there was "less hate, less division and fewer provocations" online because of "fewer bots".

Russian influence operations, which promote pro-Kremlin narratives and spread disinformation, have been tracked by researchers and journalists including BBC Verify for more than a decade.

These campaigns push disinformation on to people's social media feeds on issues like the Ukraine war or post messages in support of Moscow's interests.

Ukraine has struck three of Russian tech giant Yandex's five data centres since 8 October in response to Moscow's attacks on Ukrainian internet hubs.

The second of these strikes on Thursday caused Yandex, often referred to as Russia's Google, to announce it was struggling to maintain its services.

But claims these attacks have affected Russian disinformation operations, including accounts posting supportive messages about groups including the Make American Great Again (MAGA) movement in the US and the far-right AfD party in Germany, appear to have come from a misinterpretation of data produced by tech firm Cloudflare.

Some social media users have been sharing charts of Cloudflare data which show bot activity using Yandex's network has declined.

While bots are commonly associated with fake social media accounts that may post false, divisive and inflammatory content, they are also used to automate tasks like scanning web pages so they appear on search engines.

Cloudflare clarified its data includes all automated internet requests to websites hosted on its network, including bots crawling websites for information.

The company also said the drop off was "not necessarily bot behaviour on social media platforms".

Tomáš Zdechovský, a Czech member of the European Parliament, shared a post on X which has been viewed more than four million times, that said: "If confirmed, this is telling: Russian data centres get hit, and online activity around AfD suddenly plummets."

He has since said he "did not present it as a clear fact", but the post remains pinned at the top of his X profile.

Researchers from dTeam, a US-based group that tracks Moscow-linked influence operations, told BBC Verify there has not been "any traffic change from known Russian accounts and bot clusters on any platform".

They added that if the offices of known groups involved in these operations "were in flames then we would see a change".

Bots linked to pro-Kremlin influence operations like Storm-1516 and Matryoshka - both of which BBC Verify has previously reported on - were still active on social media on Tuesday, evidence shared with BBC Verify by dTeam shows.

Zelensky's office told BBC Verify the president was "talking about the atmosphere on social media" rather than a fall in bot activity. It added it had seen "reports of fewer provocative and hateful comments" from many social media users.

Ukraine strikes Yandex data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant

Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres

Is Burnham right to blame Russia for spreading online disinformation?

Mikhail Klimarev, an independent internet analyst, told BBC Russian that while Cloudflare can establish whether bots or real people have visited a website it does not reflect what these bots are doing.

He added that Yandex uses bots to "essentially crawl the entire internet once a day" and index websites for search engine purposes, so it is most likely the company switched these off in response to its computing resources being severely degraded.

Yandex has said the use of its cloud services for "large-scale manipulation on social media, spam and other improper activities" are against its rules and that accounts which violate this are blocked.

While there is no evidence to conclude the strikes on Yandex's data centres have had an impact on Russia's influence operations, they have disrupted internet services for many.

Isik Mater, director of research at the internet monitoring group Netblocks, told BBC Verify disruptions related to Ukrainian strikes "affect all users" globally and "websites which rely on Yandex may be partially or entirely unusable".

She said that following Ukraine's attacks there has been a clear impact on the company's cloud services and platforms relying on them, adding that an entire area remaining "out of service indicates a significant infrastructure-level incident rather than a brief service interruption".

articles.title: High tea after street heat: What happened at INDIA bloc meet at Rahul Gandhi's residence
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: INDIA bloc leaders gathered at Rahul Gandhi's residence on Tuesday for high tea amid their ongoing protest against Chief Election Commissioner
articles.body: NEW DELHI: INDIA bloc leaders gathered at Rahul Gandhi's residence on Tuesday for high tea amid their ongoing protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged vote theft. They met for a high tea after four days of protest and filing a petition in SC against the CEC.From directly slamming the CEC to criticising the SIR process and criticising PM Modi and Amit Shah, several leaders including Rahul Gandhi, Mallikarjun Kharge, Supriya Sule, Tejashwi Yadav, Sanjay Raut addressed a press conference after the meet vowing to continue their protests while giving insights into what they decided at the meeting.Here's what some of the key leaders saidRahul Gandhi (Congress)Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi anonunced that the INDIA bloc would continue its fight to restore the democratic process and ensure accountability for those he accused of undermining it. "We are all standing here together as one. As I said yesterday, there are no parallel protests. There is one singular protest, and the protest has one mission: restoration of democracy in India. Democracy has been destroyed in this country. The election system has been destroyed. The Constitution has been torn up and thrown away. We are fighting together to restore democratic rule, genuine democratic rule in this country."He thanked people who supported the protest and vowed to bring those responsible to justice. "It is our commitment to you that the people who have done this, Mr. Modi, Mr. Shah, Mr. Gyanesh Kumar, the lady who's hiding right now in Dehradun, and others are going to be brought to justice.""Yesterday, you saw an expression not of the political party standing here, but an expression of the people of India...We would like to thank the people of Delhi, the people of India, who stood with us against what is being done. This is not about us. This is about the people of India. This is about the future of the people of India, and we, all of us together, because we love you and we respect you, are going to fight to the end to restore the democratic process in this country. It is our commitment to you that the people who have done this, Mr. Modi, Mr. Shah, Mr. Gyanesh Kumar, the lady who's hiding right now in Dehradun, and others are going to be brought to justice," he added.Further assuring the work of the team, the Congress leader said, "I used the word 'perseverance' at the press conference yesterday—that this team of ours is not going to stop. Sooner or later—whether tomorrow, the day after, in three months, six months, a year, or two years—it will not stop. It will reach the end goal. I cannot tell you exactly how we will get there, because that would spoil the surprise, and we want to maintain the excitement and sense of surprise for you and the country. But I guarantee you that just as we mobilized—with such energy, strength, and unity—we will continue to fight together in the same spirit. Thank you to the Supreme Court—we have immense respect for the Supreme Court, the Chief Justice of India, and the Indian judicial system; they have a role to play, and we hope they will play it. However, we are political people; no matter what happens, or which institution plays a role or doesn't, political resistance will continue, people's resistance will continue, and it will triumph."Mallikarjun Kharge (Congress president)The Congress president hailed INDIA bloc protests against "vote chori", CEC as "massive success". "We will carry forward this united fight (protests) against Modi govt, "vote chori", he said.D Raja (CPI general secretary)Giving highlights of what they decided in the meeting, he said, "We held a meeting with senior leaders of the INDIA bloc, where we discussed the current situation in the country and how to take forward the campaign demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar."Further slamming the decision to de ntoify Jantar Mantar as a protest site, he added, "The government has now denotified Jantar Mantar. We strongly condemn this decision. Jantar Mantar must remain a place where people can protest."MA Baby (CPM)"Gyanesh Kumar has joined the ruling party's team... He steals votes, protest site and democracy," said CPI(M) leader M A Baby after the INDIA bloc meeting .Sanjay Raut (Shiv Sena UBT"(CEC) Gyanesh Kumar is a "mafia" who has criminalised entire system; we know how to fight such mafia," he said. Further talking about the meeting, he added, "Rahul ji had convened it and invited everyone—leaders and MPs were present for the high tea—and it was a very good meeting. Discussions were held, and everyone's suggestions regarding the way forward and their respective views were taken into account; however, the ongoing struggle against CEC Gyanesh Kumar, Modi ji, and Shah ji will continue—both in the national capital and elsewhere."Sagarika Ghose (TMC)She accused the Election Commission of undermining free and fair elections. She demanded a halt to the SIR process, restoration of previous electoral rolls, Kumar’s removal and criminal proceedings against officials allegedly involved in electoral irregularities."Every day, it is becoming increasingly clear that the Gyanesh Kumar-led Election Commission is undermining free and fair elections in India. As long as the Gyanesh Kumar-led Election Commission continues to function, there will be no free and fair elections in India. We stand completely united with all the leaders and parties of the INDIA alliance. We will not stop until Mr Gyanesh Kumar is removed and criminal proceedings are initiated not only against him but also against all Election Commission officials who supervised elections in Haryana, Maharashtra, Bengal and Bihar, because these have been elections marked by vote chori," she said."The government currently in power in Bengal is illegitimate. It came to power through vote chori...We have a set of demands: halt the SIR process, stop it and revert to the old electoral rolls. Gyanesh Kumar must be dismissed, and criminal proceedings must be initiated against him. All officials, who have been involved in vote chori, must be investigated, and criminal proceedings must be initiated against them. We will not rest until this Election Commission is held accountable," she added.Supriya Sule (NCP SP)Sule expressed solidarity against the CEC and stated that their agitation will continue. "We stand united with full strength as part of the INDIA alliance; our struggle will continue because the Constitution has been undermined and is currently in danger in this country. We will persist with our agitation to uphold the rights granted to all Indians in the Constitution by Bharat Ratna Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar. A single individual—representing a single government—is making a grave mistake by attempting to trample upon these rights. We stand united with full strength to fight against this injustice and oppression; our movement will continue, from Delhi down to the grassroots level," she said.Tejashwi Yadav (RJD)Taking aim at the govt said, "Govt's vote chori exposed before people. We are all together and will win." Criticising the move to remove Jantar Mantar as a protest site, he added, "Govt's fear is evident in denotification of Jantar Mantar as protest site."AISA President Neha BoraShe directly took at aim at the BJP and said, "The one enemy of the people of this country, of Indian democracy, and of the Constitution is the BJP.An attack on voter rights is an attack on India and an attack on democracy.CEC Gyanesh Kumar must go.The SIR process is compromised."Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Judge Judy fires back at critics over America remarks: ‘It’s gonna take a lot more’ to shut me up
articles.summary: Judge Judy fired back at Sunny Hostin and Ana Navarro after "The View" hosts sharply criticized her love-it-or-leave-it remarks about America.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE — Judge Judy Sheindlin responded to the furor caused by her love-it-or-leave-it remarks about America last month, explaining that she wasn’t calling America "perfect," but that the country is based on certain principles she is compelled to defend. "I have a house, and I have a home. I consider America my home," Sheindlin told USA Today in the now-viral interview exchange. "America has been good to me. I think that it’s the greatest country in the world." "If you don’t like this country, go somewhere else," she continued. "Don’t come to the greatest country in the world, the most successful country in the world, and say, ‘I want to change it.’ There are other countries that are the something else that you want. Go there. Go there. But don’t come into my home and say, ‘I want to change it.’" JUDGE JUDY SAYS THOSE WHO DON'T LIKE AMERICA SHOULD 'GO SOMEWHERE ELSE' ABC's "The View" dedicated a whole segment to Sheindlin’s take. While Sara Haines and Alyssa Farah Griffin came to her defense, Sunny Hostin and Ana Navarro expressed disappointment with the judge’s words. Hostin even said she detected "selfishness" in her comments, arguing that they focused too much on individual success. She suggested that patriotism means fighting to make your country better for everyone. "I take umbrage with what she said, and I don’t like it at all," Navarro also said of Judge Judy’s remark, adding that it’s because she loves America that she feels she has "the duty and responsibility to call out the grift and the cruelty and the racism and the abuses of power and the anti-American actions that [Trump] is taking on." Sheindlin said she didn’t understand Hostin’s response. "If you listen to what I said, I was saying my country is America," she told Fox Digital. "Every American should feel that way. And America is my home. Everybody should feel that way. So, when I said ‘my,’ I wasn’t limiting it to myself." 'THE VIEW' CO-HOST ANA NAVARRO OFFERS ONE KEY REASON FOR WHY SHE STILL IDENTIFIES AS A REPUBLICAN Of Navarro, Sheindlin said she takes everything she says with "a grain of salt." "I accept criticism, and you can criticize my view, which was not that the country is perfect — and I did say in that interview that there’s nothing wrong with tweaking this country," Sheindlin told Fox News Digital of the backlash in general. "Everything can always be better. I mean, if you live in a house — which I compared America to — if you live in a house, the house could always be better. It could use a fresh coat of paint every once in a while. Sometimes it needs new carpeting. Sometimes it will need a new stove or refrigerator to keep it functioning optimally. You have to upgrade your television sets or else you won’t be able to get certain programming and high definition. That’s tweaking." But, she added, "There’s a difference between tweaking your house and burning it down." "And this country was founded on certain principles," she continued. "And where those principles are being tested and saying those are not the right principles. I mean, if you’re a capitalistic country, you’re not a socialistic country." MORE AMERICANS THAN EVER NOW HAVE A POSITIVE VIEW OF SOCIALISM, NEW POLL SAYS "The basis of this country is a capitalist country," she continued. "And when you say, ‘Well, we don’t want capitalism anymore, we want socialism,’ that’s where I draw the line. Because then you are fiddling around with what this country is about." Socialism, she said, is not popular with the vast majority of Americans, musing that most people agreed with her statement. "The very vocal minority won’t address the statement," she said. "They try to shut you up by giving you a negative name, by calling you names which they hope will lead you to shut up. Not responding to the message and saying, ‘Judy, I understand what you’re saying, but not everyone comes from a background where they see their life being fulfilled in this country… so that everyone has potential to reach the American Dream.’" That’s an argument that Sheindlin said she understands. "But to call me a name because I said this is a great country and tweak it, but don’t burn the house down?" she asked. "It’s gonna take a lot more than Ana Navarro to shut me up," she added. Fox News Digital has reached out to "The View" for comment. JUDGE ADAM LEVY PREVIEWS HIS ‘NITTY-GRITTY’ NEW SHOW – AND HOW HIS STYLE COMPARES TO HIS MOM JUDGE JUDY "It’s one of the sad things about this internet, which has the capacity to do so many good things and join people together," Sheindlin said. "It has allowed some people, either anonymously or overtly, to be mean-spirited." Sheindlin’s special, "Judge Judy: Unfiltered, Unforgettable," aired on CBS in late September. "I think that the people who are fans over the years sort of got to know that what you see is what you get," she said. "The naysayers probably would not watch. If you’re not somebody’s cup of tea … I can skip it. I think that fans who watched the special and have been following me over the last 25 years or 30 years or newcomers for less time, I believe that they know who I am." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "My persona on my program is pretty much the same as my persona off the screen. Except that I have a family. I don’t order my family around like that the same way," she laughed. The original "Judge Judy" premiered in 1996 and ran for 25 seasons before ending in 2021. Sheindlin later launched "Judy Justice," which concluded in October. She said she was proud of the work her son, Judge Adam Levy, was doing on "Adam's Law" now that he's taken the reins of the family's TV courtroom career after Sheindlin announced she's "rewiring" her career. "I think he’s certainly smart, and he certainly works very hard at each case," Sheindlin said. "Actually, he works much harder than I did. I think he’s doing a great job and the ratings are backing him up. And I think he’s got an exciting energy and an honorable person, which is what you need behind the bench."

articles.title: Apple's new Siri-infused HomeView hub might be too little, too late
articles.summary: With Siri AI still rolling out and the original Amazon Echo Show being nearly a decade old, can Apple convince the masses that their next $299 should go towa...
articles.body:
After months of rumors, Apple is officially (and finally) making its biggest effort yet to grab a piece of the smart home pie. The iPhone maker announced the $299 HomeView on Tuesday, its first smart hub designed to put Siri front-and-center in people's homes. HomeView comes as a countertop device, or a slab you can mount to the wall, both with touchscreens, cameras and the ability to hear and execute Siri voice commands.

This is Apple's first dedicated smart home hub ever, and it supports the numerous reports suggesting the company wants to make inroads in the home space. HomeView is designed to be stationary, and it not only connects all of your compatible devices together — things like smart lights, door locks and sensors (including the new Apple Home Collection ) — but also lets you control them using either the on-screen interface or Siri voice commands.

But Apple may have a hard time convincing people to add yet another iPad-like screen to their homes, particularly one that emphasizes Siri. The new Siri, known as Siri AI , had a much delayed rollout and is only now available to users with the latest iPhones and devices running iOS 27 . Previously, Siri wasn't the most convenient voice assistant to use, nor the most helpful . Apple has a long way to go to catch up to the likes of Amazon's Alexa and Google's Assistant (now Gemini), and to make up for years of Siri being just meh. Plus, it's very late to the smart display party.

To give credit where credit is due: Apple has certainly made progress with Siri. The new Siri AI is better at answering questions with greater detail than before, and it can include personal information from your calendar, Messages and other apps in its answers. This will likely come into play with the HomeView's ability to recognize different users by their faces via the built-in camera and present personal information to them.

But doing things that Alexa and Google have been able to do for a long time is just table stakes at this point. People barely want to use Siri on their iPhones; Apple not only has to prove Siri AI is good enough for people to want to use, period, but now it also has to show it's good enough to justify a separate, $299 device. With continuously skyrocketing tech prices , this may be a particularly tough sell.

The fact that Apple is so late here is also working against the company. Amazon's original Echo Show came out in 2017, and Google's first Nest hub debuted in 2018. This isn't the first time Apple came into a space late of course — it has a habit of doing that and still coming out on top — but launching a device like this in 2026 feels a bit stale. Smart home hubs remain important for those building out connected spaces with dozens of devices, but plenty of smart home gear works over Wi-Fi now, no hub required.

Privacy could be a selling point for HomeView, and it's an area where Apple has excelled in the past. Indeed, Apple is already emphasizing the privacy aspects of HomeView: the device runs on the A18 chip and includes Secure Enclaves, which are protected and compartmentalized, and process camera and microphone data. According to Apple, data processed by Secure Enclaves "cannot be accessed by the HomeView software, apps, the user, or Apple." Siri requests on HomeView can make use of on-device processing as well as Private Cloud Compute.

Apple's $299 HomeView is available for pre-order today, and will be widely available on November 13.

articles.body: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton reportedly attended a lavish New Year’s Eve party in Dubai with two American men facing federal criminal charges in the United States, according to a bombshell report by The Wall Street Journal. The gathering took place on December 31, 2024, as fireworks welcomed 2025, and was attended by Paxton’s girlfriend, Tracy Duhon.The two men, Anosh Ahmed and Sameer Suhail, had been indicted months earlier in a federal healthcare fraud case but had not returned to the US at the time of the party, the report said. Ahmed was charged in a separate, larger alleged scheme involving at least $195 million in fraudulent government payments for Covid-19 tests. His lawyers have said in court filings that he was outside the US when the first indictment was issued and that family health issues delayed his return. Suhail’s attorney said civil matters in Dubai had affected his ability to travel and that he returned voluntarily after those matters were resolved.The party has drawn renewed attention as Paxton, a Republican backed by President Donald Trump, campaigns for a US Senate seat against Democratic nominee James Talarico. The contest has brought fresh scrutiny of Paxton’s associations, travel and past legal controversies.According to the Wall Street Journal, a video of the Dubai gathering showed Paxton and Duhon watching the fireworks from a luxury highrise balcony surrounded by other guests. Details of the event were also included in court filings in a Texas civil case.Paxton’s campaign adviser Nick Maddux did not directly address the Dubai gathering in a statement to Journal. He said Paxton had faced political persecution for years and that voters had repeatedly supported him because they believed he had fought for Texas.Paxton has faced several controversies during his tenure as Texas attorney general, including a 2023 impeachment by members of his own party over allegations of abuse of office. articles.title: Yemeni government launches air strikes on Houthi positions
articles.summary: Yemeni rights group accuses the Houthis of killing five civilians and injuring more than a dozen others.
articles.body:
Forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government say they have carried out a series of air strikes on Houthi positions and military equipment in the country’s southwest.

A total of nine air strikes were conducted in Taiz governorate on Tuesday, including five in Dhubab district and four in al-Masrakh district, the government said.

According to the Taiz Military Axis Media Center, affiliated with the Ministry of Defence, fighting is ongoing between government forces and the Houthis in al-Shaqab, south of Taiz.

The Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedom said on Tuesday that the Houthis had killed at least five civilians, including a five-year-old girl in Taiz during the previous 24 hours and injured 17 others.

The organisation accused the Houthis of shelling residential neighbourhoods, damaging at least seven homes. It also alleged that the group had fired more than 180 projectiles across Taiz during the previous 24 hours.

The war in Yemen erupted in 2014 when the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized the capital Sanaa and forced the government to flee.

An international military coalition led by Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the internationally recognised government in 2015, leading to years of fighting between the warring sides.

A 2022 UN-backed truce halted most fighting, but tensions have been high in Yemen since the Iran-aligned Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabian ports and shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandeb strait in July.

In September, the Houthis carried out a lightning ground offensive on Mocha, pushing back forces loyal to Yemen’s government from the strategic port city. The same month, the group’s forces again swept through and seized territory along the western coast and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, including the strategically located Mayyun Island in the strait.

As the fighting in Yemen continues to rage, the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, Mirjana Spoljaric, warned that civilians across the Middle East are bearing the brunt of escalating hostilities and has called for all parties to de-escalate.

“Civilians are paying an unacceptable price as a result of military operations in the Middle East,” Spoljaric said in a statement.

“In Yemen, the scale of death, displacement and damage to civilian infrastructure, including in Aden and Sanaa, is mounting at an alarming rate. Across the Middle East, civilian infrastructure has repeatedly been hit and lives have been lost,” she said.

At least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others injured in Yemen since August, many of them children, according to the United Nations.

More than 200,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since September, according to the UN’s migration agency (IOM).

As the fighting in Yemen has escalated, the Houthis have carried out a series of attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil facilities. At least 14 people were killed in separate Houthi missile attacks on King Khalid airport in Riyadh over the weekend, drawing widespread international condemnation.

Saudi Arabia’s energy minister promised the kingdom would carry out a “serious response” to the attacks.

Several airlines have cancelled flights to Saudi Arabia and neighbouring countries in response to Houthi attacks. These carriers include Qatar Airways and Emirates, the United Arab Emirates’ flagship carrier.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) on Tuesday about regional issues. Merz told MBS that Iran must engage in serious negotiations and accused Tehran of destabilising the region.

Meanwhile, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty has met Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed AlBudaiwi. Abdelatty said in a post on X that “Gulf security is integral to Egypt’s national security”.

Abdelatty also spoke to his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, and urged an immediate halt to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Although Tehran provides the Houthis with crucial financial and military support, several analysts suggest that Iran holds little sway over the group.

articles.title: ‘Not unique’: Iran seeking to expand attacks in UK to military sites, MI5 chief warns after RAF Fairford incident
articles.summary: Iran is seeking to expand its attacks in Britain to include military installations, with the suspected plot against the US-run RAF Fairford air base in
articles.body: Iran is seeking to expand its attacks in Britain to include military installations, with the suspected plot against the US-run RAF Fairford air base in September being “not unique”, MI5 chief Ken McCallum said on Tuesday.Speaking in his annual assessment of threats to the UK, the head of Britain's domestic security service said Tehran was increasingly looking beyond its traditional targets, including Iranians opposed to the country's Islamic authorities, to strike more difficult targets such as military sites.“The RAF Fairford incident ... is not unique. There have been other examples, not just in the UK but around the world,” McCallum said, according to Reuters.The comments came as British detectives continued investigating the suspected plot against RAF Fairford in western England, which has been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran during this year's war.Security alert at RAF FairfordThe suspected plot triggered a major security operation on September 27, when scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the air base as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts moved into the area.Police later said they had found a quantity of gasoline, described as an accelerant, in three vans at the site. No explosives were found.British authorities have linked Tehran to the incident, which prompted the US to withdraw its bombers from RAF Fairford.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that the suspected plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran's Revolutionary Guard.Earlier, he said that Tehran was “highly likely” to have been behind the suspected plot.Seven men in their 20s have been arrested and released on bail under investigation.McCallum said he could not comment on the Fairford incident because the investigation was ongoing. He nevertheless pointed to a broader shift in Iran's activities.“A major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites,” he said.McCallum also referred to arson and sabotage attacks on Jewish sites in Britain, which the UK has attributed to Iranian proxies. Iran has denied involvement in the suspected Fairford plot, although it has previously said it considers any military base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.MI5 flags Russia's activities and AI threatsMcCallum also warned about Russia's activities against Britain and its allies, describing Moscow as the leading state aggressor, according to Reuters.He said Russia was escalating its use of hybrid warfare against countries supporting Ukraine, employing tactics that fall short of conventional military conflict. He cited an attempted drone attack on a cargo plane at a German airport and a cyber attack on Polish energy infrastructure as examples.“It's no accident that Russian aggressors are trying to unsettle other European homelands at a time when their military progress in Ukraine is minimal and horrifically costly,” McCallum said, according to Reuters.Russia has denied involvement in hostile acts in Britain.The MI5 chief also said state threats had quadrupled over the past decade, leaving the agency devoting more resources to them than during the Cold War.He identified the potential misuse of artificial intelligence as another major security concern, particularly the risk that terrorists could use the technology to develop biological weapons or create new pathogens.McCallum's assessment outlined a range of threats facing Britain as authorities investigate the suspected Iranian plot and monitor hostile activities attributed to foreign states.You use AI every day. articles.title: Free Food Is All Around Us. The Black Forager Wants You to Find It (and Not Die)
articles.summary: Alexis Nikole Nelson, aka the Black Forager, is sharing her story, recipes and foraging tips in a new cookbook: “Happy Snacking, Don’t Die.”
articles.body: If you haven’t made Alexis Nikole Nelson’s acquaintance, you are in for a real treat. Literally. It might not be the kind of treat you’re expecting, though. It could be bread made out of acorns, fermented pine needle soda or cattail fritters. Sound a little crazy? That’s part of the fun. Nelson is the force of nature behind the Black Forager accounts on Instagram and YouTube. Dressed like a woodland fairy in her Stevie Nicks phase — long skirts, poofy sleeves, glitter, butterflies in her hair — she sings songs, sprinkles in outtakes and talks to squirrels, all in the service of teaching you about her profession and favorite pastime, foraging. She calls one of her most beloved series “America’s favorite outdoor game show: Poison or Snack.” Gathering samples of two or three common plants that are lookalikes to the casual eye, she points out the botanical details that distinguish a delightful nibble from a serious problem. And yes, there is a jingle. As hilarious as she is, she also knows her stuff. She is the botany host for John and Hank Green’s popular educational series, “Crash Course,” and has a wealth of deep scientific knowledge about nutritional and medicinal compounds in the plants growing all around us. In this tour of a single urban vacant lot, she points out remedies for sore throat, pain relievers, edible roots, egg substitutes, seeds that can be ground into flour, and the first thing her mother showed her to forage at age five: onion grass. No matter where you are in the country, you’ve probably got at least a couple of these growing right around the corner, or even in your own backyard. She’s now adding author to her list of hats, with a cookbook named for one of her catchphrases: “Happy Snacking, Don’t Die!” The book is “part foraging guide, part plant-based cookbook” and includes recipes using foraged ingredients, like color-changing Pine Shortbread Cookies, Rosewater Baklava and Juneberry Hand Pies. Widely available foods like mushrooms and acorns are heavily represented. As a dietitian, I most appreciate Nelson’s ability to model curiosity and joy about food, without falling into the traps of restriction and fear that do so much damage. She doesn’t just replace harmful food rules with better food rules; she’s using a different paradigm altogether, one of connection and community. I caught up with her to talk about that, and about what she wishes we all knew about foraging. It turned out that her wisdom didn’t come to her easily. “I was in the throes of an eating disorder when I started that Instagram,” she told me, recalling her former focus on things like lightly dressed salads and salted ramps instead of potato chips, more with the intent to interact with other foragers than to start an educational empire. “It’s interesting watching the progression of what my food on the page looked like from 2018 to now.” As she incorporated foraging into her daily life more and more, it naturally changed her relationship with food. “As I started taking more and more responsibility for the food that was ending up on my plate,” she says, “I started deconstructing this idea of good food versus bad food without even really realizing it. When you’re responsible for so much of your food, it’s so much harder for all of the accidental and purposeful moralizing of food and body to reach you. “You can’t really think of a food that you’re gathering and then preparing with your own two hands as inherently bad. It just is.” We can extend that understanding to our physical selves as well, she explains. “This body still carries me up and down mountains. This body still takes me hiking out into the woods for mushrooms and greens multiple times a week, and does everything that I require of it — dances, climbs, runs, etc,” she says. “And so if my body is still doing all of those things, then why am I feeling bad about it? “Just like food just is, our bodies just are.” From her formerly restrictive mindset, she moved to wanting to make things with what she could forage, then loosened into an overall more balanced relationship with her meals, foraged or not. “When you’re the person gathering, you do want to try a little bit of what you just spent four hours in the woods gathering,” says Nelson. Eventually, she made a pasta that’s featured in the book — Scissor-Cut Garlic Mustard Noodles — and thought to herself, “You know what? Store-bought is also fine. Thank you, Ina Garten!” It’s a good way to help encourage more adventurous eating, too, and Nelson’s advice to parents is to let kids in on foraging and cooking — with proper supervision, of course. “When I would pick dandelion flowers in our front yard and our neighbors’ kids would pick them with me, then they’re way more excited about dandelion flower fritters than they necessarily would have been,” says Nelson. “Let them participate!” She feels lucky to have had a family that encouraged her to participate herself, and although a lot of her training comes from books and an environmental science degree, her parents’ encouragement in her childhood years was formative. “Both of my parents were in scouting, which I understand, as a Black woman in America with parents who were born in the ’50s, is very, very rare,” she says, remembering gardening and foraging with her mother, and learning the constellations through a telescope with her father. “I feel very privileged in that way, from both sides.” She doesn’t expect everyone to easily follow suit, though. “I would love it if everyone who watched my content did go out and try foraging. Even just one thing, finding one wild plant that you can align yourself with the cycles of every year … but I know that not everyone is going to immediately thrift a wicker basket and go traipsing through the woods,” she laughs. “I just hope it teaches people to slow down and notice more things in their surroundings.” If you do want to add foraged foods to your repertoire, she wants to remind you of the very important second part of her cookbook title: Don’t die! Not all plants are friendly, and it’s important to have reliable information before you transfer something from the meadow to your mouth. “Starting with a book as specific to your region as possible is a plus,” Nelson explains, but she also cautions that, these days, some books you might come across are less expert and more AI. Checking a purported author’s bona fides is critical. “Us foragers and field botanists, we want to tell you everything, so if you’re having trouble finding out information, there’s not a real person there.” She also encourages finding local groups for hands-on learning, like mycology clubs that go mushroom-picking to help newbies tell a morel from a menace. Still, Nelson doesn’t think actually foraging is the only way to rekindle joy in everyday life. “Something I think that we are missing out on in a very deep-set human level in our ancient little brains, is noticing the cycles of nature around us,” she says. “Even if we live in cities, just noticing what weeds are coming up in the sidewalk cracks, how the trees in your neighborhood are behaving during different times of the year, makes so much of a difference in this very screen-driven hustle and bustle world. “Those touch points, those reminders that we were a part of something bigger than ourselves, I think are really important for humans in general. We have to exist in community, and I think that realizing that your community extends not just to the humans who live around you, but to all of the living things that live around you, makes you feel happier where you live. It makes you feel more connected to where you live; it makes you want to take better care of where you live.” Nelson left me with a favorite quote of hers to ponder, from Robin Wall Kimmerer, author of “Braiding Sweetgrass” and “The Serviceberry”: “How are you going to fall in love with the world if you don’t pick berries?” That’s a sentiment so good, I kind of wish I could eat it.

articles.title: FBI operation targets scam compounds in Africa with arrests, account takedowns
articles.summary: Operation Blackout's latest raids across Ghana and Nigeria netted 28 arrests, freed trafficked workers and saw Meta remove 3.7 million accounts.
articles.body: The FBI's expanded global efforts to disrupt and dismantle sprawling scam compounds that prey on Americans netted multiple arrests in Africa last week, as well as millions of dollars in potentially freezable funds and the takedown of social media accounts tied to fraud, officials said. Operation Blackout is the FBI’s global campaign to identify and dismantle foreign scam compounds through overseas raids, asset seizures and the disruption of web domains and infrastructure linked to scam networks. Authorities also worked to rescue trafficked workers and return stolen money to victims. "Thanks to a brilliant partnership with the Department of Justice, across multiple African countries, we arrested 28 alleged criminal actors, seized over 350 devices, identified at least $11 million in potentially freezable funds, freed over 100 trafficked workers, and identified over 100 potential scam victims here at home," FBI Director Kash Patel exclusively told Fox News Digital. FIRST ON FOX: FBI TARGETS GHANA SCAM COMPOUND LINKED TO NEARLY $10M IN LOSSES, MORE THAN 130 DETAINED "This is what happens when law enforcement executes with precision across the inter-agency," Patel added. "We are demolishing criminal scam centers across the globe and truly saving lives." In a series of initiatives stemming from the larger FBI operation, authorities conducted law enforcement raids and seizures last week as part of a "Joint Disruption Week" based out of London that resulted in 28 arrests across Ghana and Nigeria. GLOBAL PARTNERS ARE JOINING THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AND THIS FBI TO TAKE DOWN SCAM EMPIRES FOR GOOD In addition to the arrests, authorities identified more than 100 scam victims with losses so far exceeding $10 million. The more than 120 trafficked workers identified are slated to be repatriated, the FBI said. Additionally, more than 3.7 million Facebook and Instagram accounts allegedly linked to fraudulent activity were taken down in partnership with Meta. FBI WRAPS UP CYBERCRIME OPERATION TARGETING GLOBAL NETWORKS PREYING ON AMERICANS "Scams are a global threat that demand a global response," Chris Sonderby, vice president and deputy general counsel for Meta, said in a news release from the tech giant regarding last week's operations. "Working with the U.K. National Crime Agency, the FBI, DOJ and the Homeland Security Task Force, we took the fight to scam centers across West Africa. "As part of the disruption, we removed more than 3.7 million accounts, Pages and Groups targeting people in the U.S., U.K., and beyond, and shared leads on over 30 suspected scam centers resulting in dozens of arrests, the rescue of trafficking victims and cryptocurrency seizures," Sonderby added. GLOBAL TASK FORCE DISMANTLES 'PIG-BUTCHERING' CRYPTO FRAUD RINGS PREYING ON AMERICANS In Ghana, 117 victims are pending repatriation to Nigeria, and 19 suspects were arrested and detained. In Nigeria, local authorities will prosecute nine individuals arrested for violations of Nigerian law, the FBI said. The Ghana and Nigeria operations follow a warning from Patel that international scam networks were expanding beyond Southeast Asia and the Middle East into Africa. "That’s why you’re seeing the migration of these scam compounds to central and sub-Saharan Africa, which is where we are already pre-positioned to take them off," Patel told Fox News Digital in September. The FBI-led initiative targets transnational cybercrime groups operating massive scam centers where trafficked workers are forced to carry out fraud schemes from thousands of miles away against unsuspecting Americans. AMERICANS LOST OVER $20 BILLION TO ONE TYPE OF CRIME. HERE’S HOW WE CAN FIGHT IT In total, Operation Blackout has resulted in roughly $17 billion being seized, hundreds of alleged scammers arrested and thousands of trafficked workers freed. Furthermore, more than 10,000 Americans were warned about being targeted for potential fraud before losing their money, preventing an estimated $670 million in financial losses, according to the FBI. Many of the victims are senior citizens, Patel previously told Fox News Digital. Criminal networks have begun a geographic shift in an effort to broaden their scams, Patel has said. BURMA APPROVES DEATH PENALTY FOR SCAMMERS MONTHS AFTER FBI'S $8 BILLION CRYPTO CRACKDOWN In September, a Justice Department Scam Center Strike Force team helped authorities in Madagascar take down 13 scam centers operated by Chinese organized crime syndicates and process more than 3,200 electronic devices, Fox News Digital previously reported. Criminal networks have now begun using artificial intelligence to further their scams, experts said. The technology gives scammers the ability to use voice cloning and send flawless emails and messages to potential victims, eliminating the language barriers that once made scams easy to spot. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "AI gives scam fighters powerful new tools," said Jack Stubbs, the lead scams investigator at OpenAI. "At OpenAI, we’re using AI to disrupt scam operations and help people spot scams. By sharing insights responsibly with industry and law enforcement partners, we can identify scam networks across platforms and build stronger collective defenses." articles.title: Why has search of Ilhan Omar’s home before US midterms caused controversy?
articles.summary: Federal agents searched Omar’s home in what she described as an attempt to ‘weaponise federal law enforcement’.
articles.body:
United States federal agents have searched the Washington, DC home of Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar , a Muslim and a prominent critic of President Donald Trump, as part of an investigation that one source said was linked to alleged immigration fraud.

The predawn raid on Monday came three weeks before the US midterm elections on November 3, in which Omar is seeking a fifth term representing Minnesota’s 5th congressional district.

Omar called the raid an attempt to “weaponise federal law enforcement”, while top Democrats said the timing raised “serious questions”.

So why has the search caused such alarm? Here’s what we know:

Agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), executed what the US Department of Justice called a “judicially authorised search warrant”.

The department said only that it was part of “an ongoing federal investigation”.

The street around Omar’s home was blocked off on Monday morning, and agents were seen removing boxes labelled “Seized Property Evidence”.

Hours later, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with the search, saying it was “really up to the DOJ [Justice Department]”.

However, a person described as familiar with the investigation told the Reuters news agency that it relates to alleged immigration fraud, and that part of it concerns paperwork filled out by Omar’s late father when she was a child.

Omar fled Somalia’s civil war with her family when she was aged eight.

According to her House biography, the family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before moving to the United States in the 1990s. She became a citizen in 2000.

Conservative websites have for years alleged that she “married her brother” to commit immigration fraud, claims Omar has dismissed as “disgusting lies”.

US Vice President JD Vance said in March, without offering evidence, that the administration believed Omar “definitely committed immigration fraud”. Her office called the claim fabricated and defamatory.

Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told conservative podcaster Benny Johnson that “something’s going to happen” in the case.

“If we can prove that you shouldn’t have been here in the first place, we’ll deport you,” he said.

Justice Department policy usually avoids taking any action whose timing would appear to affect an election or benefit a candidate or party. In practice, therefore, the department has historically avoided overt investigative steps against candidates within about 60 days of a vote.

Randall Eliason, a law professor at George Washington University and former federal public corruption prosecutor, said the raid appeared to break with that practice, though there is no way to enforce the policy.

“The idea is to avoid even the appearance of any kind of interference by the Department of Justice with the political process,” he said.

The norm’s most famous test came in 2016. On October 28, 11 days before the presidential election, then-FBI Director James Comey told Congress that the bureau was examining newly discovered emails linked to its investigation into Hillary Clinton’s private email server.

Clinton has blamed this, in part, for her defeat. A 2018 review by the Justice Department’s inspector general found Comey’s conduct “extraordinary and insubordinate”.

Electorally, little appears to hang on the outcome. Omar represents a very safe Democratic seat covering Minneapolis, which she won in 2024 by 50 percentage points.

On November 3, she faces Republican Dalia al-Aqidi, an Iraq-born former journalist who has called Omar “pro-Hamas”, in a rematch of the 2024 race.

The search fits a wider pattern, however. During Trump’s second term, the Justice Department has charged several of his perceived political enemies, including Comey himself, New York Attorney General Letitia James and former National Security Adviser John Bolton.

She claims she is being targeted as one of Trump’s “political enemies”.

“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns,” she wrote on X. “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”

Omar has previously described Trump’s focus on her as an “unhealthy and creepy obsession”, and says she and her family have received death threats that she blames on his rhetoric.

In early December last year, Trump took aim at the Somali community in Minnesota and called Somali immigrants “ garbage “. “We’re going to go the wrong way if we keep taking in garbage into our country. Ilhan Omar is garbage. She’s garbage. Her friends are garbage.”

In January, a man sprayed her with vinegar at a town hall in Minneapolis. Anthony James Kazmierczak, who admitted attacking her because he disagreed with her progressive views, was sentenced last month to 14 months in prison.

Trump, meanwhile, returned to Omar’s origins at a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, on Monday this week.

“She comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet,” he said, as the crowd chanted: “Deport.”

What are Democrats and other critics saying?

That the raid on Omar’s home is an abuse of power.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, joined by Representatives Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar, called the raid “deeply disturbing”.

Trump’s “mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family”, they said, promising to “deliver full accountability”.

Minnesota Governor Tim Walz said Trump was “abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election”.

Few Republicans have commented publicly. One who did, Representative Nancy Mace, wrote that if fraud was proven, Omar “should be denaturalised and removed from this country”.

Questions have also been raised about internal checks. A person familiar with the investigation told Reuters the department consulted its Public Integrity Section, which has historically approved investigations of members of Congress, before the search.

The Trump administration has cut the Public Integrity Section to about two lawyers as part of the sweeping government cuts he introduced after taking office in January 2025. Before that, the unit had 35 to 40 full-time lawyers.

articles.title: 911 operators questioned whether Christa Pike failed execution call was prank, audio reveals
articles.summary: 911 audio reveals dispatchers initially dismissed Christa Pike's failed execution as a prank call, delaying the ambulance response to Riverbend Prison.
articles.body: 911 dispatch recordings show a series of miscommunications led to delayed emergency response in the immediate aftermath of the Tennessee Department of Correction’s failed execution of death row inmate Christa Pike. An initial 911 call came through to dispatchers around 8:40 p.m. on Sept. 30, roughly an hour after Pike’s planned execution began, according to documents and audio recordings obtained by Fox News. During the call, the unidentified caller informed operators of a failed execution but was unable to provide the operators with a code that would verify the legitimacy of the call. Following that call, operators sought to determine the authenticity of the audio shows. TENNESSEE DEATH ROW INMATE SURVIVES 2 LETHAL INJECTION DOSES IN FAILED EXECUTION ATTEMPT "So we have a medical call for service at the Riverbend Prison," a dispatcher says in the Fox News-obtained audio. The dispatcher explains to another operator that the caller said, "They carried out the execution, the subject didn’t pass away, and they need an ambulance because she’s not breathing normally." DEATH ROW INMATE UNCONSCIOUS ON VENTILATOR AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION FOR TEEN’S KILLING: ATTORNEYS "We are trying to find out if that is an actual thing that is happening, and we need to send an ambulance, and/or if you need police assistance, or if this is someone that is just basically prank calling or like swatting us," the operator can be heard saying. In another snippet of internal dispatcher audio, an operator can be heard calling off the emergency response. TENNESSEE PRISON CHIEF RESIGNS AFTER FAILED EXECUTION AS FORMER US ATTORNEY TAPPED TO LEAD INDEPENDENT REVIEW "Per supervisors here at the DEC [Department of Emergency Communications], we have been informed it is a false call," a dispatcher can be heard saying at approximately 9:03 p.m. "There is no medical assistance needed at Riverbend Prison." An additional correspondence between an operator and what appeared to be somebody working at Riverbend Prison displayed further confusion. CHRISTA PIKE'S FIRST WORDS REVEALED AFTER SHE UNEXPECTEDLY WOKE UP WHILE LAWYERS THOUGHT SHE WAS 'BRAIN DEAD' "We got a call about a failed execution at your guys’ facility, and we’re just calling to verify," a dispatcher said. "Um … who called you?" the prison employee responded. "Is there like a sergeant I could speak with, or a supervisor?" the dispatcher asked. "Who called you? Do you know?" the employee said. "No, we don’t exactly know," the dispatcher replied. "I’m being told nobody from our facility called you, so there’s not really anything to speak of at the moment," the employee said. CHRISTA PIKE NOW CONSCIOUS AND TALKING AFTER SURVIVING 2 DOSES OF LETHAL INJECTION DRUG Pike’s attorney Kelly Gleason also called 911 to report the botched execution, audio recordings prove. "What’s going on is my client, Christa Gail Pike, is undergoing a state execution. She has completed the stages of the protocol and last we knew from the attorney who is present, she is still alive and breathing and needs immediate life-saving care," Gleason can be heard saying during a phone call timestamped at approximately 9:08 p.m. CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEY SAYS SHE'S 'UP AND WALKING' MORE THAN A WEEK AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION Around the same time as Gleason’s call, Riverbend Prison’s Central Control told emergency responders that they "would have been the ones to call in" but that they "did not make that call," according to the audio. But also around that time, a first responder can be heard on a separate recording saying: "Somebody is outside the gate at the prison telling us that it’s real and demanding us to go in. They say they are some sort of state official. I need somebody to get out to the gate and talk to those people." At that point, Central Control cleared the way for first responders to enter the prison at 9:11 p.m. Pike was in an ambulance and being transferred to a hospital by 9:34 p.m., the Associated Press reported. Pike was convicted of first degree murder and conspiracy to commit first degree murder in 1996 for the 1995 torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. She was sentenced to death and had been on death row for over 30 years when she arrived at her scheduled execution by lethal injection on Sept. 30. Prison execution authorities administered a single dose of pentobarbital, a central nervous system depressant used in Tennessee execution protocol. When Pike remained conscious after the initial dose, authorities administered a second dose per state protocol. When the second dose did not kill Pike, Tennessee’s single-drug execution protocol prevented authorities from administering a third dose. Pike was taken to a hospital where she was placed on a ventilator and remained unconscious for six days, waking up on Oct. 6, according to her attorneys. Pike was taken back to the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center women’s prison on Oct. 10 where she is continuing to receive medical care, her attorneys said in a statement. Following the failed execution, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has paused all state executions pending a further review. articles.title: Sunak meets Modi, hails his leadership as UK-India ties go ‘from strength to strength’
articles.summary: Former UK prime minister Rishi Sunak met Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi on Tuesday and congratulated him on completing 25 years in public
articles.body: Former UK prime minister Rishi Sunak met Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi on Tuesday and congratulated him on completing 25 years in public service. Praising PM Modi’s commitment and work ethic, Sunak said the UK-India relationship was going from “strength to strength” under his leadership.In a post on X, Sunak recalled working with PM Modi during his tenure as prime minister and highlighted the importance of closer cooperation between the two countries in trade, technology and artificial intelligence (AI).“Prime Minister Narendra Modi great to see you in New Delhi today. Congratulations on 25 years in public service, a remarkable achievement. It was a pleasure to work with you when I was Prime Minister,” Sunak wrote.Praising Modi’s approach to public service, he added, “Your commitment, your work ethic, your energy is an example to us all.”On bilateral ties, Sunak said, “The UK India relationship is going from strength to strength under your leadership. Our two countries cooperating more on trade, tech and AI is vital in a less predictable world.”He also expressed confidence in the future of the partnership, writing, “I know that Britain and India will continue to grow ever closer in the years ahead.”Earlier on Tuesday, Sunak spoke about the changing global order and the growing ability of countries such as India and those in the Gulf to pursue independent foreign policy positions amid increasing geopolitical uncertainty.Speaking at a panel discussion titled “The End of Predictability” at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026 in New Delhi, Sunak said the world was moving away from the multilateral, rules-based framework that had shaped the global economy.“We all grew up investing in, operating in a multilateral rules-based framework, largely enforced by US President Trump is not a cause for that; he's a symptom of that, and the world that we're in now is one where we don't quite know what we've settled down to, and that creates an enormous amount of geopolitical uncertainty and indeed danger,” he said.Sunak also described China’s emergence as a strategic competitor to the United States as a significant shift.“So, China is a peer competitor for the US across economic, military, and technological domains. That is a new feature of the world economy,” he said.Meanwhile, India and the UK have agreed to exchange annual data on the utilisation of tariff concessions under their Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA). The decision was taken at the 16th meeting of the India-UK Joint Economic and Trade Committee (JETCO) in New Delhi on Monday.Commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal and UK business secretary Jonathan Reynolds reviewed progress since the agreement came into force on July 15, 2026. The annual data exchange is intended to support smoother implementation and help more businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, benefit from the pact.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Block, blunt, break’: What’s in NATO’s new Russia war plan?
articles.summary: NATO’s top commander says he is revealing a plan to stop a Russian invasion of Europe.
articles.body:
NATO’s top general has unveiled a new war plan for countering a Russian attack on members of the alliance, embedding lessons learned from the front lines in Ukraine.

Speaking about NATO’s so-called “theory of victory” at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, General Alexus Grynkewich, who has served as head of United States European Command and the Supreme Allied Commander Europe since 2025, said the plan rests on three strategies designed to stop an invasion in its tracks: “block, blunt and break”.

The announcement comes amid mounting warnings from European intelligence agencies of rising threats from Russia, including both the prospect of conventional military action and “hybrid warfare”, which can include tactics from cyberattacks to tampering with undersea cables.

In a bid to ease the alliance’s growing concerns, Grynkewich said: “What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we’ve got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it.”

But the new plan from NATO comes at a time when the alliance itself appears divided on how to deal with Russia, following a series of recent overtures from US President Donald Trump to Russian President Vladimir Putin, including his latest controversial plan for Russia to release stocks of diesel to global markets despite sanctions on Russian oil.

So, what’s in the new NATO plan, and what are European agencies warning about? How has Russia reacted? And is the alliance even on the same page on all of this?

General Grynkewich told the Warsaw Security Forum that NATO does not view a military confrontation with Russia as “imminent or inevitable”, but that it will nevertheless be ready for one.

“Implementing the theory of victory I’ve described today would require me to issue orders that I hope to never give,” he said. “But let there be no doubt: should war come, we will block, blunt any attack, and then if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us.”

The “block, blunt and break” strategy, he explained, is aimed at stopping an attack rather than taking enemy territory.

Drawing directly on lessons learned on the front lines in Ukraine and from conflict in the Middle East, Grynkewich said the plan relies on the use of precision weapons with “affordable mass”, like drones, and other autonomous systems.

In the plan, he said, the alliance’s forces would “block” an attack at the border to halt enemy advances on the battlefield, then “blunt” the attack by hitting incoming troops from the air, sea, and land. Then, at last, they would aim to “break” the enemy by targeting the supply chain and command networks.

“If required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us,” he said. “Enemy formations will be starved of replenishment. Enemy commanders will be unable to control their forces. Enemy forces and support capabilities will be reduced and destroyed.”

Are Russian threats in Europe on the rise?

Germany’s foreign intelligence chief, Martin Jaeger, warned last week that the country risked being drawn into a “violent conflict” with Russia, saying Moscow increasingly viewed Berlin as a principal adversary.

He cited an attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport in August as an example of the escalating threat. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has also warned of a Russian-linked “shadow war” involving sabotage, cyberattacks and other covert operations.

In France, President Emmanuel Macron warned last month that the Russian hybrid threat facing France and other European countries had intensified in recent weeks, and ordered the preparation of plans to protect critical infrastructure.

The United Kingdom’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that he had received confirmation upon entering office that Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum , although he did not publicly detail the evidence behind that assessment. Last week, he travelled to Berlin to meet with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz , in part to discuss plans to combat Russian hybrid warfare.

Russia issued a nuclear warning to NATO late last month, saying it was prepared to use its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave bordering Poland and Lithuania.

In July, Romania’s Defence Ministry said it had recorded 33 instances of Russian drones entering its airspace since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. Eighteen of those incursions had occurred this year, and Romanian F-16 fighter jets had shot down three drones during the year.

Poland has also accused Russian intelligence services of orchestrating an arson attack on a Starlink satellite-internet station in Wola Krobowska last month. Warsaw described the incident as part of Russia’s hybrid warfare campaign against countries supporting Ukraine.

Norway, too, has issued similar warnings. Beate Gangas, head of the country’s Police Security Service, said this week that Europe is facing its most serious security situation since World War II, echoing concerns over suspected Russian sabotage and covert operations across the continent.

In August, Russia warned the UK that it could face “consequences” for supplying drones to Ukraine that have been used in long-range attacks inside Russian territory.

“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which ⁠it will have to answer,” the Russian embassy in London said in a statement on August 17. “The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kyiv’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.”

Despite this, Russia is not preparing for “any kind” of conflict with Europe, President Vladimir Putin said last month. He added that Russia had “no real motive” to escalate tensions and criticised European countries that have suggested otherwise.

“Many in Europe talk about expecting an attack from Russia and therefore believe they must themselves prepare for hostilities, for a war with Russia,” Putin told reporters in St Petersburg.

“I want to emphasise once again: we are not preparing for any kind of hostilities with Europe,” he noted.

Putin added that Russia was considering its stance on whether to resume peace talks with Ukraine following recent Ukrainian attacks on Russia, particularly on energy infrastructure.

“On proposals to resume negotiations, yes, they are all on the table, and it is all possible. But after everything they’ve done, we will give careful thought to what steps we need to take in response,” Putin said.

Since taking presidential office in the US, Trump has repeatedly attacked other NATO members for not shouldering enough of the financial burden for defence. He has also been angered by NATO members’ general refusal to join in the US-Israel war on Iran.

As a result, there are fears that Trump cannot be relied on to provide support if it is needed within the NATO alliance, analysts say.

In August, after the Russian consulate in London warned of “consequences” for the UK for providing Ukraine with long-range drones, former Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Fedorov told the BBC that could include the possibility of attacks. He said many of the military experts currently advising the Kremlin are “convinced” that NATO would not respond forcefully if Russia were to hit the UK. “Trump will not allow NATO to answer,” he said.

The alliance is facing a deepening divide over Russia, as Trump pursues engagement with Moscow while European governments insist that Russia must remain under pressure if the war in Ukraine is to come to an end.

Last month, Washington invited Putin to December’s Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami, in a move that was seen as potentially ending Moscow’s diplomatic isolation since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The European Union responded that Russia remained a G20 member but said it would continue condemning the invasion regardless of whether Putin attended.

The divide deepened last week when Trump announced a deal allowing Russian diesel exports into US and global markets, temporarily easing sanctions on Russian fuel. His administration said the move could help lower energy prices and encourage Putin to return to peace negotiations.

Critics have warned that it would generate revenue for Russia while undermining Western efforts to constrain its war effort.

Meanwhile, Trump has also escalated his criticism of Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and suggested that Ukraine should elect a new leader willing to make a deal with Russia. Zelenskyy had called Trump’s diesel agreement with Putin “not fair and not honest”, arguing it would benefit Russia.

EU foreign ministers also insisted that European sanctions against Russia would remain in place despite Washington’s deal with Moscow.

On Sunday, Trump claimed in a Truth Social post to have instigated an “energy truce” between Russia and Ukraine, under which both sides would refrain from targeting each other’s energy facilities with long-range strikes. However, Zelenskyy said such a deal was “news to me” – although he also said Ukraine would respect such a truce if Moscow honoured it as well. Regardless, Russia, which also has not confirmed agreeing to an energy truce, continued striking Ukraine’s facilities on Monday, according to Ukrainian officials.

articles.title: Sweden’s centre-left leader fails in second bid to form government
articles.summary: Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson says ‘conditions not in place’ to form government, prolonging deadlock.
articles.body:
The leader of Sweden’s left-wing Social Democratic Party, Magdalena Andersson, has said her efforts to form a government have failed, prolonging a political deadlock a month after parliamentary elections.

Speaking at a news conference Tuesday, Andersson said talks with the three other parties in the country’s left-wing bloc had hit an impasse.

Despite progress, she said she did not believe conditions were in place to “form a government that can be tolerated by parliament”.

It is her second time failing to form a government after Sweden’s parliamentary vote on September 13.

Shortly after the announcement, the country’s parliament speaker, Andreas Norlen, who had tasked Andersson with gauging conditions to form a government, said a vote on whether to make Andersson prime minister would proceed in parliament on Thursday. He conceded that Andersson would likely fail to pass the vote.

Under the Swedish system, a prime minister can secure office so long as a parliamentary majority does not vote against them.

Sweden’s centre-left opposition bloc narrowly defeated outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s right-wing bloc in last month’s election, winning 176 seats to the right-wing bloc’s 173. However, Andersson’s bloc has struggled to form a government due to competing terms from several of its members. The Centre Party has said it will oppose a government that includes cabinet posts for the Left Party, which has in turn insisted it will only support a left-wing government of which it is a member.

If Andersson fails in Thursday’s vote, Norlen is expected to ask Kristersson, who currently leads a caretaker government, to hold negotiations with other parties.

Speaking to reporters, Norlen said he considered Kristersson a potential next candidate, but the speaker did not wish to commit to that too soon and would “respect the process”.

To succeed, Kristersson would need to convince an opposition party to support him or at least not vote against him.

The speaker of parliament has four attempts at proposing a prime minister for parliament to vote on. If the fourth attempt fails, a snap election must be called.

After Sweden’s 2022 election , negotiations to form a government took more than a month, and those following the 2018 election lasted more than four months.
